title: Project: implement and review a dispatch queue UI
summary: Turn a fictional dispatch brief into a reviewed, responsive, accessible UI change.
body:
Implement a fictional Dispatch Queue from an approved screen brief and one desktop screenshot. The fixture contains 47 shipments, 6 on hold. Build a status filter, visible-result count, and row list. Deliver a component inventory, interaction contract, responsive state matrix, rendered review packet, and test results. Leave shipment actions outside this change. The screenshot supplies visual evidence but no authority about hidden states, URL persistence, or control semantics.

Plan the implementation boundary

Inspect existing Select, list-row, typography, spacing, and focus patterns. The queue page owns filter selection and fetch state. Reuse the Select if it can express the approved behavior. Record whether the filter belongs in the URL as an unresolved product decision until confirmed; keep the initial implementation local if no routing behavior is specified. All shows 47 visible records and Held shows 6. Loading is pending work, empty means a successful query returned no matches, and error means data could not be obtained. Do not turn the error into a misleading count of zero.

Build the state and access matrix

Check a wide All state, a narrow Held state with a long destination, a narrow empty search, and a narrow request error. The filter and Retry controls need names, keyboard access, and a visible focus state. Keep headings and rows in a logical reading order. Compare each rendered state with the approved visual intent, then test filter transitions and error recovery separately. A screenshot does not reveal those interactions. If an existing shared Select must change, identify every consumer and run regression checks there too.

Fixture: All 47; Held 6; other status counts are unspecified.
States: loading | result | empty | request error.
Acceptance: count = visible successful result, never a failed fetch.
Widths: wide All; narrow Held with long text; narrow empty/error.
Access: named controls, keyboard path, visible focus, reading order.
Release packet: captures, state assertions, affected consumers, fixes.

Performance and operating cost

Filtering N loaded rows costs O(N) per selection; a copied visible list costs O(N) additional space. If production data is paginated, the server owns filtering and the count must describe the returned scope or a verified total. A complete V-by-S screenshot grid costs O(VS) captures, so choose representative states by distinct failure risk. Run cheap state assertions before image comparisons. The reviewer should reject a visually close screen if the error state lies about data, the filter cannot be used by keyboard, or a shared component change lacks consumer checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer URL state or pagination from a desktop image.
  • Do not copy pixels at the expense of semantic controls and natural reflow.
  • Do not approve a polished error screen that reports a successful empty result.

Visible appearance at that state and width

title: Document prompts: define the reader's decision before drafting
summary: Specify audience, decision, scope, evidence packet, and editable deliverable.
body:
A document-production prompt is a contract for a decision artifact. Define who will read it, what decision the reader must make, which evidence packet is allowed, what is excluded, the required file format, and the review gate. The prompt should identify the claim types it may make: observed counts, interpretations, and proposed actions. A polished narrative cannot repair an unclear denominator or an absent decision owner. Ask for an outline before laying out pages, then require each section to answer a reader question. Preserve editability with actual headings and paragraphs in the requested document format; a page image that looks right is not an editable report.

Operational case

North Quay's fictional maintenance board needs to decide whether to authorize a follow-up review of overdue inspections. Its frozen packet contains 47 inspection records: 38 current, 6 overdue, and 3 pending validation. The report can state those counts and identify the six overdue records. It cannot call the three pending records completed or overdue without new evidence. The board asks for a short editable report, not a recommendation to replace equipment. The document brief names the operations lead as decision owner and marks equipment replacement outside scope. A reviewer can reject a persuasive page that hides the pending category or silently broadens the requested decision.

Reader: North Quay maintenance board.
Decision: authorize a follow-up review of 6 overdue records.
Packet: 47 inspections = 38 current + 6 overdue + 3 pending.
Deliverable: editable report with heading hierarchy and decision box.
Excluded: equipment replacement proposal; status guesses for pending.
Gate: reconcile counts and inspect rendered pages before release.

Performance and operating cost

Outlining costs one additional drafting pass, but reduces layout rework caused by late changes to purpose. For N records, count reconciliation is O(N) and should happen before the model writes conclusions. A short report still needs page-by-page inspection because one wrapped heading or clipped note can change the meaning of a decision box. Keep the prompt brief proportional to the decision; copying every raw record into the model can increase cost and exposure without improving the board's view.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not let the document's tone imply a decision beyond the authorized question.
  • Do not collapse pending validation into current or overdue.
  • Do not substitute a flattened page image for an editable report.

title: Report prompts: reconcile every claim with the packet
summary: Keep an internal claim ledger with evidence IDs, arithmetic, and unresolved records.
body:
A report claim ledger maps each material statement to a permitted evidence item or calculation. It is an internal verification record, not a demand to expose private source material in the published report. The prompt should distinguish a raw observation, an arithmetic result, and a judgment. Require exact units, denominator, and status definitions for every count or rate. If records disagree, retain the conflict and name the owner who can resolve it; do not select the more convenient value. Reconcile totals deterministically before drafting and recheck every number after editing, because a late wording change can turn a correct count into a misleading claim.

Operational case

The North Quay packet has 47 records. A worksheet says 38 current, 6 overdue, and 3 pending validation; the sum is 47. A draft sentence says 'nine inspections need immediate action' by adding overdue and pending. That arithmetic is valid as a combined count but its label is not: pending validation is not the same as overdue. The ledger rejects the sentence. It accepts 'six overdue inspections require follow-up; three statuses await validation.' A chart showing 6 of 47 overdue must keep 47 as its denominator and label pending separately. If a second sheet reports seven overdue, the discrepancy remains open until a record-level reconciliation identifies the difference.

Claim C1: 47 records in frozen packet; verify record IDs are distinct.
Claim C2: 38 current + 6 overdue + 3 pending = 47.
Claim C3: overdue share = 6/47, approximately 12.8%.
Blocked: '9 require immediate action' conflates two statuses.
Conflict: second sheet says 7 overdue -> hold claim for record review.

Performance and operating cost

A single pass over N records builds counts in O(N) time and O(K) space for K status buckets; a record-ID check may require O(N) additional space. A claim ledger adds one review decision per material statement, but makes corrections cheaper than rereading the full report after every revision. Arithmetic should be performed by a deterministic calculation or spreadsheet cell, not trusted to an unverified prose generation. Reconcile the final exported file too; correct draft text does not prove the output artifact retained the correct numbers.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not turn a valid sum into an unsupported operational category.
  • Do not calculate a rate without naming its denominator.
  • Do not conceal a conflicting count by selecting the first sheet.

title: Editable report prompts: inspect structure and rendered pages
summary: Use real heading styles, preserve text editability, and catch page-level defects.
body:
An editable-report prompt should specify both logical document structure and rendered appearance. Use actual title and heading styles, meaningful text rather than images of paragraphs, descriptive labels for figures, and a reading order that matches the intended flow. Define page constraints such as margins, repeated headers, and where a decision summary may split. After generation, render every page and inspect it at reading size for clipping, orphaned headings, footnotes that drift from their claim, and charts too small to read. Text extraction checks whether expected words exist; rendered inspection checks whether people can use the page. Neither check alone is sufficient.

Operational case

North Quay's report contains a decision summary, count reconciliation, an overdue-record list, and a pending-validation note. A generated page places the pending note in a narrow callout; its last line is clipped in the PDF preview. Text extraction still finds the words, so a text-only check would pass. The layout is repaired, then all pages are rerendered. The heading hierarchy is checked in the editable file rather than inferred from bold text. The figure describing the 38/6/3 split gets a purpose-based text alternative that states the values without duplicating an adjacent paragraph word for word.

Structure: title -> decision summary -> counts -> overdue records -> limits.
Editable file: heading styles, selectable paragraphs, labeled figure.
Render gate: inspect every page at reading size.
Text gate: expected counts and pending note remain extractable.
Failure: clipped callout -> repair layout -> rerender all pages.

Performance and operating cost

Rendering P pages and checking their text is at least O(P) page operations; image inspection also scales with pixel area. A change to a shared header or style can affect every page, so rerender the whole document after that edit. Manual review focuses on high-risk page boundaries, figures, and footnotes rather than reading every line twice. A smaller font may hide overflow but can make the report unreadable; fix the underlying layout or shorten the content with the decision owner instead.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate bold text with a real heading hierarchy.
  • Do not approve a file from text extraction while its rendered note is clipped.
  • Do not shrink type to conceal overflow without checking readability.

title: Slide prompts: one claim, supporting evidence, usable order
summary: Build a presentation from verified claims, with readable visuals and intentional speaker notes.
body:
A slide-deck prompt should specify the audience, meeting decision, claim per slide, supporting evidence, and what belongs in speaker notes. The deck is a different reading surface from the report: it should not paste paragraphs onto slides or suppress important caveats to create visual space. Each visual needs units and an explanation that survives without color alone. The file should retain editable text and a logical object order for assistive reading. Verify the slide's claim against the report ledger after every edit. Speaker notes may add context, but must not hold the only statement of a material limitation that changes the visible claim.

Operational case

North Quay requests a six-slide briefing. Slide two states 'Six of 47 inspections are overdue' and shows all three categories: 38 current, 6 overdue, 3 pending. Its first draft used a red segment for overdue without a text label, so the category was unclear without color. The revision adds labels and counts. A later slide asks for authorization to review the six overdue records; it does not recommend replacing equipment. The notes explain that the three pending records await validation, while the visible slide also states this limit. Reading-order inspection finds the chart title after the chart, and the order is corrected before release.

Slide 1: decision and scope.
Slide 2: 47 = 38 current + 6 overdue + 3 pending.
Slide 3: six overdue records and proposed review owner.
Slide 4: three pending validations; no assumed status.
Slide 5: review timeline and open questions.
Slide 6: authorization requested; limitations visible.

Performance and operating cost

For S slides and C material claims, verification is O(S+C) review steps when the ledger indexes claims by ID. Rendering and inspecting all S slides adds O(S) image operations, with extra time for charts and reading-order checks. Reusing the report's verified numbers reduces contradictory edits, but an automated copy can still move a caveat into notes or lose a category label. A dense deck may save slide count while increasing comprehension cost; trim by decision relevance, not by hiding uncertainty.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not paste the report into slides and call it a presentation.
  • Do not make a category depend on color alone.
  • Do not bury a limitation in speaker notes while the visible claim overstates certainty.

title: PDF export prompts: verify the delivered file again
summary: Check exported text, page appearance, navigation, and claim consistency before delivery.
body:
A PDF export is a new artifact with its own failure modes. A release prompt should name the source file, export method, expected page count or range, required text, and manual checks. Verify selectable text, document structure or tags where supported, reading order, descriptive alternatives for meaningful figures, and visible layout on every page. Do not assume the source application's accessibility checks automatically carry through conversion. Compare the exported report's counts and decision statement with the approved claim ledger and editable source. If the PDF is flattened or loses structure, repair the export path or clearly withhold that artifact rather than describing it as accessible.

Operational case

North Quay's editable report passes its own review. The first PDF export preserves 47, 38, 6, and 3 as text, but moves a footnote to the next page and leaves the chart out of the reading order. The PDF is not released. The team adjusts the source layout and export settings, exports again, inspects each page, and checks structure in the actual PDF. The final delivery packet retains the editable report, six-slide deck, PDF, claim ledger, and a short note of tested limitations. A request for equipment replacement approval would require a new brief; no formatting check can authorize it.

Source: approved editable North Quay report.
Export checks: text selectable; 47/38/6/3 present; pages inspect clean.
Structure: heading order, figure alternative, logical reading order.
Cross-file: report, six slides, and PDF use the same claims.
Release: owner reviews actual files; failed PDF is withheld.

Performance and operating cost

With P PDF pages, visual and text checks take O(P) page passes, plus a small set of cross-file claim comparisons. Structural inspection takes longer when a chart or multi-column layout has a complex reading order. Re-export after source edits and rerun checks on the new file; a previous PDF pass does not transfer to changed bytes. Hashing the approved artifact is O(B) for B bytes and gives a stable receipt for which exact file was reviewed, though it does not prove the file is correct.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer PDF accessibility from a clean source document alone.
  • Do not release a flattened PDF that only appears readable in a screenshot.
  • Do not reuse an earlier approval after the exported bytes change.

title: Project: deliver a North Quay maintenance briefing
summary: Draft and verify one decision across an editable report, six-slide deck, and PDF export.
body:
Produce a decision packet for the fictional North Quay maintenance board. The frozen input contains 47 distinct inspection records: 38 current, 6 overdue, and 3 pending validation. The board can authorize a follow-up review of the six overdue records; equipment replacement is outside this brief. Deliver an editable report, a six-slide briefing, a PDF export of the report, an internal claim ledger, and a release checklist. The project assesses the prompt contract and verification process, not a real maintenance decision.

Define the claims before formatting

Record C1 as 47 distinct inspections, C2 as the 38/6/3 split, and C3 as six overdue inspections requiring review. If a rate is useful, 6 divided by 47 is approximately 12.8%, with 47 named as the denominator. The three pending records stay unresolved; do not combine them with overdue under an 'immediate action' label. A conflicting spreadsheet count of seven overdue pauses that claim until record IDs are reconciled. The report decision summary must ask for a review, not for replacement funding.

Create and inspect each artifact

Build the report with real heading styles and editable text. Render every page and check the decision box, chart alternative, footnotes, and long record labels. Build six slides with a visible claim per slide, labeled categories, and a logical object order; notes may add context but cannot hide the pending-validation limit. Export the approved report to PDF, then inspect the actual PDF for selectable text, clean pages, structure, and reading order. A clean source file does not waive export checks. Keep the claim ledger and exact reviewed artifact identities with the packet.

Frozen input: 47 = 38 current + 6 overdue + 3 pending.
Decision: authorize review of 6 overdue records only.
Report: editable headings, decision summary, limitations, page review.
Slides: six claims with labels, visible caveats, reading-order check.
PDF: export from approved report, inspect text, pages, and structure.
Release: reconcile all three files to C1-C3 and record tested limits.

Performance and operating cost

Record reconciliation is O(N) over N inspection rows. Claim review is O(C) for C material claims when each has a ledger entry. Rendering a P-page report and S-slide deck is O(P+S) artifact passes before inspection time; the PDF adds another O(P) pass. Recheck the exact files after any edit because an earlier screenshot or accessibility pass applies only to the earlier bytes. The expensive failure is a convincing packet whose numbers or decision boundary differ across formats.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not promote pending validation into an overdue status.
  • Do not move a material limitation entirely into speaker notes.
  • Do not approve a PDF merely because the editable report passed review.

title: Meeting prompts: define authorized inputs and evidence
summary: Bound transcript access, distinguish notes from speech, and retain uncertain spans.
body:
A meeting-record prompt begins with an input boundary. Name the meeting, authorized transcript and notes, access scope, intended recipients, and retention rule. Treat the transcript as evidence about what was said, not as proof that a plan was approved. Speaker labels and timestamps can be wrong; ask for a traceable span and mark uncertain attribution rather than assigning a statement to the nearest name. The system that captures or shares a meeting must apply its recording and access policy outside the prompt. A recap generator should receive the minimum permitted excerpt needed for its task and should not silently combine another meeting, chat thread, or private document.

Operational case

In a fictional Beacon API pilot meeting, five attendees discuss a limited deployment to 20 depots. The permitted packet contains the transcript and chair's notes for that meeting only. One sentence at 12:43 is partly inaudible and the transcript labels its speaker as Dana, but the chair's notes do not confirm it. The prompt marks the speaker as uncertain; it does not turn the sentence into Dana's commitment. A separate private staffing note is excluded. The recap is prepared for the five attendees to review before it reaches the larger delivery group. The prompt's access instruction cannot itself grant or revoke transcript permissions.

Meeting: Beacon API pilot; audience: five attendees.
Allowed: this meeting's transcript and chair notes only.
Excluded: private staffing note and other meeting threads.
Span 12:43: attribution uncertain; do not assign an owner.
Output: draft recap for attendee correction before wider share.

Performance and operating cost

Scanning T transcript turns and N note items is O(T+N) work before summarization. Long recordings raise token cost and increase the chance that a late decision is buried; segment by agenda item while preserving time and speaker context. Keeping evidence span IDs beside draft claims adds storage proportional to the number of claims, but saves review time when someone disputes a decision. Retention and access rules need enforcement in the meeting system; removing a transcript from a prompt does not delete its stored copy.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer consent to record or share from a prompt instruction.
  • Do not assign an inaudible statement to a named person without confirmation.
  • Do not merge private notes into a recap for a wider audience.

title: Meeting minutes: separate decisions from proposals
summary: Classify each statement as approved, proposed, rejected, or unresolved with its evidence span.
body:
A decision ledger prevents a recap from promoting discussion into policy. For every proposed change, record the exact decision question, status, approving authority, evidence span, and any condition. Use distinct labels for approved, proposed, rejected, and unresolved; a confident speaker or silence after a suggestion is not an approval. Preserve material disagreement when it changes the next step. If the transcript and chair's notes conflict, mark the item for attendee review instead of selecting the cleaner story. Draft minutes should state what the meeting established and what remains open, using short sentences that a participant can confirm or correct.

Operational case

Beacon's chair approves a pilot in 20 depots after rollback validation. A participant proposes rolling out to all 47 depots in the same week, but the chair says the wider rollout is outside today's decision. Another attendee asks whether the pilot can start without the rollback test; no answer is recorded. The recap lists the 20-depot pilot as a conditional decision, the 47-depot rollout as a proposal not approved, and the missing rollback-test answer as unresolved. It does not write 'Beacon rollout approved' because that headline would erase the scope and condition. The approval span is retained for attendee review.

D1 approved conditionally: 20-depot pilot after rollback validation.
P1 proposed, not approved: expansion to all 47 depots.
O1 unresolved: may pilot start before rollback test?
Evidence: retain transcript spans and chair-note comparison.
Headline: pilot decision, not full rollout approval.

Performance and operating cost

Classifying M material agenda statements is O(M) initial passes, followed by human review of disputed or high-impact entries. A compact ledger is cheaper to correct than a long narrative whose assumptions are woven through several paragraphs. Do not use a vote count unless the meeting actually recorded a vote and its rules. Classification quality matters more than compression ratio: an extra line that preserves a condition is less costly than a brief recap that sends a team toward an unauthorized rollout.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not label a proposal as approved because it went unchallenged for one minute.
  • Do not omit a condition from the decision headline.
  • Do not erase dissent when it changes who must review the next step.

title: Meeting actions: verify owner, task, and due date
summary: Keep unassigned work unassigned until a named owner accepts it.
body:
An action item is an agreed task with an owner, deliverable, and due point or explicit absence of one. A prompt should extract these fields separately and require evidence for each. A person's question about a task does not assign them the task; a phrase such as 'someone should check' produces an unassigned item. Do not invent calendar dates from 'soon' or map a month/day to a year without meeting context. When owner or deadline is missing, label it missing and ask the meeting chair or participant to confirm. If the application creates tickets, the recap remains a draft until the owner and target system are authorized.

Operational case

In the Beacon meeting, Dana accepts the rollback validation and says she will send the test result by 10 October 2026. The chair asks who will notify the 20 pilot depots, but no one accepts that task. The ledger records Dana's action with its date and leaves depot notification unassigned with no deadline. The transcript's uncertain 12:43 utterance cannot be used to fill the gap. A generated ticket for Dana's task still needs an authorized submission step and a receipt from the ticket system. The recap does not claim the task is complete merely because a ticket was drafted.

A1: Dana; rollback validation result; due 10 Oct 2026; accepted.
A2: notify 20 pilot depots; owner missing; due date missing.
Do not use uncertain 12:43 speaker to fill A2.
Draft ticket != submitted ticket; require receipt after authorized create.

Performance and operating cost

Extracting A candidate actions from T turns can be O(T+A) if candidates retain span pointers. Verification time rises with ambiguous ownership, but that is the cost of not assigning work to the wrong person. Cross-check due dates against the meeting date and time zone when deadlines matter. Ticket creation has an external side effect; validation, authorization, and receipt reconciliation add steps beyond text generation. Keep the output small enough for attendees to correct each action before it enters a work queue.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assign a task to the person who merely asked about it.
  • Do not translate 'soon' into a precise deadline without confirmation.
  • Do not call an action complete because a draft ticket exists.

title: Meeting recaps: preserve corrections across sessions
summary: Track what changed, who confirmed it, and which earlier decision remains in force.
body:
A recurring-meeting recap should carry forward only confirmed decisions and open actions, with their versions and owners. The prompt must not treat a newer meeting as a blanket replacement for all prior minutes. A correction may change the wording of one action, revoke a decision, or merely add context. Record the original claim, corrected claim, confirming person, and effective meeting. If two sessions conflict, show the conflict until an authorized owner resolves it. In the next recap, distinguish completed, still open, superseded, and newly assigned actions. This keeps the record usable without pasting entire transcripts into every prompt.

Operational case

One week after Beacon's pilot meeting, a follow-up says the rollback validation passed and Dana's action is complete. The 20-depot pilot may proceed. The 47-depot expansion is still unapproved. The chair corrects an earlier recap that had mistakenly named Dana as owner of depot notification; the action returns to unassigned until Jo accepts it in the follow-up. The revision ledger retains the old wording, the correction, and the meeting where Jo accepted. It does not silently overwrite the earlier minutes or assume the full rollout became approved because the pilot condition cleared.

Prior D1: 20-depot pilot conditional on rollback test.
Follow-up: rollback passed -> condition satisfied; pilot may proceed.
Prior P1: 47-depot expansion remains unapproved.
Correction: notification owner Dana -> unassigned -> Jo accepted.
Record each state change with confirming meeting and reviewer.

Performance and operating cost

With H historical decisions and actions, a bounded carry-forward ledger needs O(H) storage; replaying all prior transcript tokens for every meeting grows much faster as the series lengthens. Diffing K changed entries is O(K) after identifiers match. A version ledger adds review work but prevents an attractive recap from erasing accountability. Archive closed actions according to the organization's retention policy instead of carrying them forever. A model summary can suggest what changed; the meeting owner confirms the operative state.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not overwrite an earlier record without an explicit correction trail.
  • Do not treat fulfillment of a pilot condition as approval for full expansion.
  • Do not carry a guessed owner into the next meeting as settled fact.

title: Meeting recap release: review scope, access, and corrections
summary: Verify every decision and action before sharing a recap beyond participants.
body:
A meeting recap is ready for release only when the permitted audience, decision ledger, action owners, due dates, unresolved items, and sensitive material have been reviewed. The prompt can produce a draft and a verification checklist; it cannot authorize recipients, change recording consent, or send the recap by itself. Ask the chair or designated reviewer to inspect high-impact decisions and participant-attributed commitments. Send a correction route with the released record so attendees can contest an error. If a correction changes a ticket or published plan, update that downstream artifact through its own authorized workflow and record the receipt.

Operational case

Beacon's draft correctly lists a conditional 20-depot pilot, an unapproved 47-depot proposal, Dana's rollback task, and an unassigned notification task. Before wider distribution, the chair checks the evidence spans and removes a private staffing remark from the summary. Dana confirms her due date. The draft remains with attendees until the chair approves the recipient list. After release, Jo corrects the notification owner and accepts it; the correction is recorded in the next version. A ticket is created only after the work system's approval gate and its receipt is linked to the action ledger.

Check: D1 condition; P1 not approved; A1 owner/date; A2 unassigned.
Remove: private staffing remark outside the recap's audience.
Review: chair approves claims and recipient list.
Correction route: attendee reports error; version and downstream ticket updated.
Send only after authorized release; retain delivery receipt.

Performance and operating cost

For D decisions, A actions, and R proposed recipients, release review requires O(D+A+R) checks before downstream effects. Human approval adds delay but targets the points where a wrong attribution or unauthorized disclosure has the greatest cost. Keep the shared recap concise and store evidence spans in a restricted review packet; publishing every transcript quote to all recipients expands exposure. Sending and ticket creation are separate side effects, each needing its own success receipt and correction path if later information changes.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not interpret a generated draft as permission to email recipients.
  • Do not release a private remark because it appeared in the authorized transcript.
  • Do not correct the recap while leaving a contradictory downstream ticket in place.

title: Project: review a Beacon pilot meeting record
summary: Separate a pilot decision from a proposal and carry corrected actions into a reviewed recap.
body:
Draft a reviewed record for a fictional Beacon API pilot meeting and its follow-up. Five attendees discuss a 20-depot pilot, a possible expansion to 47 depots, rollback validation, and depot notification. The permitted packet is the meeting transcript and chair's notes; a private staffing note is excluded. The deliverables are a decision ledger, action ledger, attendee-review draft, correction record, and release checklist. No real recording, email, or ticket is created by this exercise.

Classify the first meeting

The chair conditionally approves the 20-depot pilot after rollback validation. Expansion to 47 depots is proposed but not approved. Whether the pilot could start without a test remains an open question in the transcript and must not silently become approval. Dana accepts the rollback test result due 10 October 2026. Depot notification has no accepted owner or due date. An utterance at 12:43 has uncertain speaker attribution, so it cannot fill those missing fields. Every material entry keeps an evidence span for participant correction.

Carry corrections into the follow-up

The follow-up confirms the rollback test passed, satisfying the pilot condition. It does not approve the 47-depot expansion. Jo accepts depot notification, correcting an earlier draft that had guessed Dana as owner. The revision ledger retains the old draft, correction, confirming meeting, and current action state. Before sharing the recap beyond attendees, the chair reviews decisions, owner and date fields, recipient access, and the removal of the private staffing remark. A ticket can be submitted only through an authorized work-system step, with its receipt linked back to the action.

D1: 20-depot pilot; conditional approval; rollback test required.
P1: 47-depot expansion; proposed, not approved.
A1: Dana; rollback test result; due 10 Oct 2026.
A2: depot notification; unassigned -> Jo accepts in follow-up.
Uncertain span: 12:43 speaker unknown; no invented commitment.
Release: chair reviews audience, claims, corrections, and side effects.

Performance and operating cost

For T transcript turns and A action candidates, evidence extraction is O(T+A) with span pointers. Carrying a bounded ledger of H open decisions and actions uses O(H) state between sessions instead of resending every transcript. Review adds one check per material decision, commitment, and recipient. That work is justified by the risk of turning a proposal into a rollout or assigning a task to the wrong person. The final recap remains a draft until the chair approves it; text generation cannot grant access or prove a ticket was submitted.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate discussion with approval.
  • Do not guess an owner from an uncertain transcript segment.
  • Do not send or create tickets merely because the recap prompt asks for them.

title: Architecture prompts: start with constraints and an owner
summary: Define the decision, workload, quality targets, constraints, and missing measurements.
body:
An architecture prompt should name one decision, the person accountable for it, the current system, observed workload, quality targets, non-negotiable constraints, and facts still unknown. Ask the model to distinguish measurements from estimates before it proposes a design. A diagram is not a decision: it can show components while hiding why a queue, database, or retry rule is needed. Record the client-visible behavior, data correctness rule, failure tolerance, and operational budget. If the input lacks a measured service rate, the prompt should request a load test or return a conditional comparison rather than inventing capacity. Keep the proposed design scoped to the decision actually requested.

Operational case

A fictional Receipt Ingest service accepts 18,600 requests per minute on a normal business day. Product wants to choose whether to add a queue before the receipt writer. A burst multiplier of 2.4 is a planning assumption, not an observed peak. Each request has an identity key so retries must not write two receipts. The engineering lead owns the decision; operations must review a worker-failure plan. The prompt asks for response-time and loss targets but marks both as missing until the teams set them. It does not treat the normal traffic figure as proof that one worker can handle the peak.

Decision: direct writes or bounded queue before receipt writer.
Observed: 18,600 accepted requests/minute in normal period.
Assumed: 2.4x planning burst; validate against traffic traces.
Invariant: one durable receipt per request identity.
Owner: engineering lead; operations reviews failure behavior.
Unknown: latency target, loss tolerance, measured worker capacity.

Performance and operating cost

Capturing the brief takes a few review turns but avoids modeling a workload that has not been defined. For N requirements, a claim ledger is O(N) entries; the hard part is verifying the numbers and resolving conflicts, not writing the entries. A short list of unknowns can prevent expensive redesign after a benchmark disproves an assumption. Do not turn a budget into a target without specifying the time window and measurement point. The model may organize the decision, while the accountable engineer approves its scope.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call an assumed burst factor an observed peak.
  • Do not propose a queue without stating which failure or latency constraint it addresses.
  • Do not make the model the decision owner.

title: Capacity prompts: check units, headroom, and a failed worker
summary: Turn stated traffic and measured throughput into a reproducible capacity estimate.
body:
A capacity prompt should show each unit conversion and assumption before it recommends an instance count. Separate sustained demand, burst demand, measured sustainable capacity per worker, and reserve for an unavailable worker. Use a deterministic calculation for integer rounding. The number is a planning lower bound under the stated workload, not proof that latency, database capacity, or network limits will hold. Ask which resource saturates first and what load test would falsify the estimate. When the worker benchmark is missing, leave the denominator blank instead of dividing by a fabricated throughput.

Operational case

Receipt Ingest sees 18,600 requests per minute, or 310 per second. Applying the assumed 2.4 burst factor gives 744 requests per second. A load test under the same request mix measures 47 sustainable requests per second per healthy worker. The peak therefore needs 16 healthy workers because 15 provide only 705 per second, while 16 provide 752. To retain 16 after one worker fails, deploy 17. This ignores database, queue, and network limits until separate tests verify them. The estimate must be revised if the 2.4 factor or measured worker rate changes.

from math import ceil

normal_requests_per_minute = 18_600
planning_burst_factor = 2.4
measured_worker_rps = 47
failed_worker_reserve = 1

peak_rps = ceil(normal_requests_per_minute / 60 * planning_burst_factor)
healthy_workers = ceil(peak_rps / measured_worker_rps)
deployed_workers = healthy_workers + failed_worker_reserve
assert (deployed_workers - 1) * measured_worker_rps >= peak_rps
print(f"peak_rps={peak_rps} healthy_workers={healthy_workers} deployed_workers={deployed_workers}")

Performance and operating cost

The arithmetic is O(1) time and space for fixed inputs; measurement and load testing dominate effort. At 47 requests per second, 16 healthy workers provide 752 per second, only eight above the planning peak, so the team should test burst duration, uneven routing, and downstream saturation before treating this as safe headroom. A queue can absorb a transient mismatch but adds storage, delay, and replay behavior. The prompt must state whether the arrival rate counts retries, because retries can raise offered load during failures.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not round down a fractional worker requirement.
  • Do not add a failed-worker reserve and then forget to evaluate capacity after that worker is gone.
  • Do not claim end-to-end capacity from a worker-only benchmark.

title: Architecture decisions: compare real alternatives and consequences
summary: Record the direct-write and queued designs against the same constraints.
body:
An architecture decision prompt should compare plausible alternatives under identical workload and correctness assumptions. Record what each option gains, what it costs, its failure behavior, and the evidence needed before acceptance. Avoid a feature checklist in which one option is given the best implementation and the other a straw version. Name which consequences are reversible and which require data migration or client contract changes. A decision record may be proposed, accepted, or superseded; a new choice should preserve the reason the earlier one was made. The model can draft the comparison, but measured tests and an accountable reviewer settle the decision.

Operational case

For Receipt Ingest, direct writes keep a simple request path and can return a durable result immediately, but a writer slowdown may push latency or failure to clients. A bounded queue can absorb short bursts and decouple acceptance from processing, but it changes the meaning of 'accepted' and requires backlog monitoring, replay rules, and a dead-letter path. Both need request-ID deduplication to avoid duplicate receipts. The prompt asks whether a client needs a final receipt in the same response; if so, queueing cannot be treated as equivalent without a new status contract. The engineering lead proposes one option only after a load test and client review.

Option A: direct write; simple response; writer failure reaches client.
Option B: bounded queue; async completion; backlog and replay duties.
Shared invariant: request ID yields at most one durable receipt.
Open contract: does HTTP acceptance mean complete or enqueued?
Decision status: proposed until client and load evidence are reviewed.

Performance and operating cost

Comparing O alternatives against C constraints takes O(OC) explicit checks. The matrix is small; quality depends on using the same evidence for both options. Queueing adds storage proportional to arrival rate multiplied by backlog duration, plus worker and operational cost. Direct writes avoid that queue but may need spare writer capacity for burst traffic. A model should state these costs as conditional rather than pretend to price a system without retention, traffic mix, or infrastructure rates.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not compare a complete queue design with an unrealistically weak direct-write design.
  • Do not equate enqueue acknowledgement with a durable completed receipt.
  • Do not erase a superseded decision and its reason.

title: Architecture prompts: test the failure path and its signals
summary: Tie overload, retries, and dependency faults to observable user outcomes.
body:
A failure-mode prompt should enumerate the events that could break the chosen design, the user-visible effect, the signal that detects it, and the recovery step. For a queued system, examine duplicate delivery, full queue, poisoned message, worker loss, and downstream unavailability. For direct writes, examine request timeout after a successful commit and retry behavior. The prompt should require bounded retries and an explicit point where human operators take over. Observability is not a list of dashboards: each metric or trace must answer a recovery question. Define what is measured at the client boundary, because an internal healthy worker count can coexist with failing requests.

Operational case

Receipt Ingest's proposed queue accepts a request, then the writer fails for 90 seconds. New requests may enter the bounded queue only until its capacity is reached. The prompt requires queue depth, oldest-message age, acceptance failures, duplicate-suppression count, and end-to-end completion latency. A poisoned record moves to a reviewed failure path after a bounded retry count; it must not block every later receipt. Recovery replays by request ID so a duplicate delivery cannot produce a second durable receipt. An operator must know when backlog age exceeds the agreed target and whether the system is still accepting work it cannot complete.

Fault: writer unavailable for 90 seconds.
User effect: accepted receipt may remain incomplete; queue may fill.
Signals: acceptance failure, oldest age, depth, completion latency.
Recovery: bounded retry; isolate poison; replay by request ID.
Escalation: stop accepting beyond bounded capacity and page owner.

Performance and operating cost

At a planning peak of 744 requests per second, a complete 90-second writer outage could add 66,960 arrivals before retries or rejection, if admission remains open and no work drains. That is a scenario calculation, not a recommended queue size; capacity must also account for payload bytes, burst duration, and recovery drain rate. Tracking M in-flight identities needs O(M) state until retention or compaction. A prompt that asks only for 'high availability' misses the concrete backlog and duplicate behavior operators must test.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not describe queue depth as proof of completed receipts.
  • Do not retry a poison record forever.
  • Do not accept more work than bounded storage and recovery policy permit.

title: Architecture release: require evidence, rollback, and ownership
summary: Stage the change against load, correctness, and recovery checks before expansion.
body:
An architecture release prompt should turn a proposed decision into an evidence packet: load-test workload, correctness checks, failure injection, operational signals, rollout stages, stop conditions, rollback method, and named owners. The prompt must not declare a design production-ready from a diagram or a single arithmetic estimate. State which hypothesis each test addresses and what result would block release. A rollback may restore old traffic routing while queued work remains, so the plan must say who drains, replays, or quarantines in-flight records. An accepted decision record and a deployed change are separate states; approval does not prove rollout occurred.

Operational case

The Receipt Ingest lead chooses a limited queued pilot only after clients accept the asynchronous completion contract. A load test uses the measured 47-request-per-second worker mix and the 744-request-per-second planning peak, then checks completion latency and database load. A failure test removes one of 17 deployed workers and confirms the 16 survivors can sustain the target under the tested mix. Another test replays duplicate request IDs and interrupts the writer. The pilot starts with a small traffic slice; expansion stops if oldest-message age or duplicate receipt count breaches the agreed threshold. Operations owns rollback and the in-flight queue disposition.

Gate 1: client accepts enqueue-versus-complete response contract.
Gate 2: 744-rps load mix; database and latency within agreed limits.
Gate 3: one worker lost; 16 healthy workers sustain test.
Gate 4: duplicate and writer-failure tests preserve one receipt/ID.
Pilot: small traffic slice; stop thresholds and queue disposition named.
Status: accepted ADR != completed rollout; record deployment receipt.

Performance and operating cost

A staged rollout costs extra test environments, observation time, and operational review, but bounds the number of users exposed to a wrong assumption. If R rollout stages each run K checks, review work is O(RK), plus recovery drills. Reusing the same workload definition across tests makes comparisons meaningful. The queue's backlog after rollback can outlive the routing change, so the team must budget time and capacity to drain it safely. Record both passing and failing runs; a selective success trace cannot justify expansion.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use a clean diagram as evidence of load or failure behavior.
  • Do not rollback routing without a plan for already accepted queued work.
  • Do not report an accepted decision record as proof of a completed deployment.

title: Project: review a receipt-ingest architecture decision
summary: Compare direct writes and a bounded queue using checked capacity and recovery evidence.
body:
Write a reviewable architecture decision for a fictional Receipt Ingest service. The service normally accepts 18,600 requests per minute. A 2.4 planning burst is assumed; the measured worker throughput is 47 requests per second under the relevant mix. Each request identity may produce only one durable receipt. Compare direct writes with a bounded queue, including what a client response means in each design. Deliver an assumption ledger, verified capacity estimate, proposed decision record, failure exercise, and staged release gate. The engineering lead owns acceptance; operations reviews recovery.

Calculate before comparing

Normal traffic is 310 requests per second, and the assumed burst is 744 per second. A worker measurement of 47 per second yields 16 healthy workers at peak, with 17 deployed if one may be unavailable. This is a worker-only planning bound; test the database, network, traffic mix, and latency separately. A complete 90-second writer outage at 744 arrivals per second could produce 66,960 arrivals before retries or rejection if admission stays open. That scenario makes queue capacity and admission policy explicit rather than recommending an untested size.

Compare and test the two contracts

Direct writes can return a completed receipt in the request path but expose writer slowdown to clients. A bounded queue can absorb a brief mismatch but may return only an enqueue acknowledgement; the client must accept a later completion state. Both paths require request-ID deduplication. The proposed queue decision stays unaccepted until client contract review and load evidence exist. Test duplicate replay, poisoned work, full queue behavior, and one failed worker. During a small pilot, stop expansion if completion latency, oldest-message age, or duplicate receipts breach the agreed limits. A rollback plan must account for already accepted queued work.

Observed normal: 18,600/min = 310/s.
Assumed peak: 310 x 2.4 = 744/s.
Measured worker: 47/s; 16 healthy; 17 deployed for one loss.
Writer outage scenario: 744 x 90 = 66,960 arrivals.
Open: client response contract, database capacity, latency target.
Release: limited pilot, stop limits, rollback owner and queue plan.

Performance and operating cost

Fixed-input capacity arithmetic is O(1); checking N workload records to validate the traffic assumption is O(N). Comparing two options across C constraints is O(C), while R release stages with K checks require O(RK) review actions. These counts say nothing about actual production safety without representative load and failure measurements. The final record should distinguish measured, assumed, proposed, accepted, deployed, and superseded states so no diagram or model response appears to authorize a rollout.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not present 17 workers as an end-to-end guarantee.
  • Do not treat queue acceptance as completed receipt delivery.
  • Do not rollback routing while leaving in-flight work without an owner.

title: API documentation prompts: bind prose to a versioned contract
summary: Read the endpoint, schema, tests, and version before drafting an API page.
body:
An API documentation prompt should receive a bounded evidence packet: the relevant operation contract, implementation behavior, integration tests, and version policy. Identify which artifact defines the public contract when code and schema disagree. The model may draft an explanation, but it must not invent a parameter, status code, response field, or permission from surrounding conventions. State the exact endpoint version and change under review. Ask for a discrepancy ledger before prose if a test and specification differ. Separate public behavior from internal class names; readers need the contract they can call, not an unreviewed dump of source code.

Operational case

A fictional Shipment Status API adds the status held to version two of its shipment response. The endpoint is GET /v2/shipments/{shipmentId}. The approved operation contract allows queued, in_transit, held, and delivered. One old guide lists only three values, while an integration test has a held fixture. The prompt first records that drift and asks the API owner to confirm that held is released in v2. It does not infer that a new hold_reason field exists just because the implementation stores one internally. The public page will be drafted only against the confirmed contract and test fixture.

Scope: GET /v2/shipments/{shipmentId}; version 2.
Packet: approved operation contract, handler behavior, integration tests.
Change: held joins queued, in_transit, delivered.
Conflict: old guide lacks held -> record drift and confirm release.
Unknown: internal hold_reason is not automatically public.

Performance and operating cost

Reading E endpoint artifacts and T relevant tests is O(E+T) inspection work. Restricting the prompt to the changed operation reduces token cost and prevents an unrelated endpoint from contaminating the example. A discrepancy ledger takes extra review but is cheaper than publishing an invented field across several pages. A generated page must be checked against the authoritative contract after editing; a good opening paragraph does not validate every request and response detail.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not document an internal field as public without contract evidence.
  • Do not copy an older guide as the only truth when its enum is stale.
  • Do not mix behavior from different API versions.

title: API prompts: document the full operation matrix
summary: Specify inputs, success and failure responses, permissions, and retry behavior.
body:
An API operation page should describe how a caller forms a request and interprets every documented outcome. The prompt must enumerate method, path parameters, authentication scope, successful response shape, material error codes, and retry guidance supported by the service contract. A happy-path body alone leaves integrators to guess what happens when an ID is missing or access is denied. The prompt should label fields that are required, optional, or conditionally present and keep null distinct from absent. If the source packet does not establish an error code or retry policy, mark it for owner review instead of filling the gap with a familiar convention.

Operational case

For GET /v2/shipments/{shipmentId}, the approved contract requires shipmentId and a reader permission. The successful response has shipment_id and status; the held fixture uses SH-4721 and status held. A not-found result is documented as 404 with a structured code. The security test proves a caller without the reader permission receives 403. The prompt leaves a timeout retry rule open until the API owner confirms it. It does not show a 200 response with status delivered for a missing ID, and it does not treat 403 as evidence that the shipment does not exist.

GET /v2/shipments/{shipmentId}
Required path: shipmentId; permission: shipment:read.
200: shipment_id, status; held fixture SH-4721.
403: caller lacks read permission.
404: shipment ID not found under approved visibility rule.
Retry on timeout: unresolved until owner confirms policy.

Performance and operating cost

For R response classes and F documented fields, a complete review is O(R+F) contract checks per operation. Authentication and error tests often cost more to inspect than the success fixture, but they prevent misleading integration instructions. A generated error matrix should be checked against actual tests or approved specification, not merely against another generated page. Omitting unknown retry behavior can be safer than prescribing retries that amplify an outage or duplicate a side effect.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer 404 versus 403 behavior without checking visibility rules.
  • Do not call an optional field required because it appears in one fixture.
  • Do not invent retry advice from a status code alone.

title: API examples: validate payloads and strip credentials
summary: Use deterministic fixtures, run examples, and keep private values out of docs.
body:
A documentation example should be a verified contract case, not a plausible-looking JSON object. The prompt must identify the fixture or test that supplies each field, use fictional identifiers, and omit live credentials and personal data. Validate the example against the released schema, then run a request or contract test in a safe environment where practical. Check that printed output agrees with the status description and version. For a request requiring authorization, use a clear placeholder rather than a valid token. The review should catch accidental copy of production IDs, access keys, internal hostnames, and sample values that imply a field exists when it does not.

Operational case

The held-shipment page includes SH-4721 as a fictional ID. Its 200 response shows shipment_id and status held, matching the approved fixture. An earlier draft inserted hold_reason and a long authorization token copied from a debug log; both are removed. The contract does not expose hold_reason, and the token is not safe to publish. The reviewer runs the example against a local fixture and confirms the JSON parses and the two public fields have the right types. A 403 example uses a fabricated error code already present in the permission test, not a copied customer response.

Request ID: SH-4721 (fictional fixture).
200 JSON: {"shipment_id":"SH-4721","status":"held"}
Authorization: <reader-token> placeholder only.
Reject: internal hold_reason, live token, production identifier.
Check: JSON parse, released schema, fixture output, version.

Performance and operating cost

Parsing an example of B bytes is O(B) and schema validation depends on the schema depth and field count; a single local fixture run is usually cheap compared with a published integration error. Secret scanning adds a pass over the draft and generated files. The prompt should not claim that one valid example proves the whole operation correct; negative cases and permission boundaries need separate tests. Keep examples few and distinct so each teaches a meaningful branch rather than repeating the success body with new IDs.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not publish a real token as a convenient example.
  • Do not add a field because it appears in an internal log.
  • Do not trust syntax-only JSON validation as proof of contract alignment.

title: API changes: explain client impact and migration
summary: Classify compatibility from client behavior, not only schema shape.
body:
An API change prompt should describe the before and after contract, supported versions, affected clients, rollout timing, and test evidence. Adding an enum value can look additive in a schema while breaking clients with exhaustive status handling. The prompt should ask how callers treat unknown values and whether a versioned migration note is required. Record the old behavior, new behavior, fallback for clients that cannot update immediately, and owner of each compatibility claim. Do not announce a deprecation or date unless the release policy approves it. A migration note is a change guide, not a substitute for the current operation page.

Operational case

Shipment Status v2 adds held. One client maps every known status to an icon with no default branch; held causes that client to fail despite being an added enum value. Another client displays unknown statuses as 'Status unavailable' and continues. The prompt documents both outcomes and asks the API owner whether to gate held behind a version boundary or coordinate the client release. The draft migration note tells callers to handle unknown status values and adds a held fixture to contract tests. It does not claim that every client is safe because the response still uses a string.

Before: queued | in_transit | delivered.
After: queued | in_transit | held | delivered.
Client A: exhaustive mapping -> fails on held.
Client B: unknown fallback -> remains usable.
Gate: choose version/release plan; add held contract fixture.
Do not invent deprecation date or universal compatibility.

Performance and operating cost

With C known client integrations and S changed status values, targeted compatibility review is O(CS) behavior checks. Unknown external clients add uncertainty; publish a conservative migration note and monitoring plan rather than claiming total coverage. A coordinated release may slow delivery, but it avoids turning an apparently harmless schema addition into a client outage. Keep version and behavior claims tied to the actual deployment state; a merged contract change is not proof that every environment serves held.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate additive schema shape with safe client behavior.
  • Do not promise a retirement date the release plan has not approved.
  • Do not report held as live in every environment from a merged test alone.

title: API docs release: test links, examples, and live version
summary: Reconcile published pages with the deployed contract and preserve a review trail.
body:
An API documentation release prompt should name the target version and environment, affected pages, internal links, example fixtures, contract checks, owner approval, and rollback path. A docs build can succeed while pointing readers to a stale enum page or a newer endpoint that is not deployed. Validate internal links and navigation, run sample payload checks, and compare the published claim with a deployment receipt or approved release record. If docs publish before the service, label the future behavior clearly or defer the page. Keep a change ledger so a later release can tell which examples and migration notes need revision. Do not let the model itself declare production behavior from code that has not shipped.

Operational case

The Shipment Status v2 draft links to a shared status-values page that still lists three values. Link checking reports a valid destination, but a content check detects the stale enum. The editorial owner updates the values page and reruns its link and example checks. The v2 operation page, held fixture, and migration note remain in review until the deployment record confirms held is served. A staged environment may serve held earlier; the page must label that environment instead of implying public availability. After release, a client report that held is mishandled opens a correction to the migration guidance and a tracked follow-up.

Check pages: operation, status values, migration note.
Check links: targets resolve and describe the same version.
Check examples: parse, schema, fixture, secret scan.
Check release: deployment receipt confirms held in target environment.
If mismatch: hold or label staged behavior; record correction owner.

Performance and operating cost

For L links and X examples, basic verification is O(L+X) checks, plus contract tests and a deployment-state lookup. Automated link checks catch missing targets but not semantically stale destinations, so reviewers inspect version-sensitive pages. Publishing a correction costs less when the change ledger identifies affected examples and status lists. A rollback of docs must not erase a truthful migration warning for clients already seeing held; the owner decides whether to patch text, change routing, or coordinate a service rollback.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a resolving link as proof that its target is current.
  • Do not publish a future endpoint as live without a deployment receipt.
  • Do not fix one operation page while leaving a shared enum page stale.

title: Project: review Shipment Status API documentation
summary: Align one versioned shipment endpoint, examples, migration note, and release state.
body:
Update the fictional Shipment Status API documentation for GET /v2/shipments/{shipmentId}. The confirmed version-two contract adds held to queued, in_transit, and delivered. The held fixture is SH-4721. The public success response includes shipment_id and status; an internal hold_reason field is not in the public contract. The deliverables are an operation page, checked example, compatibility note, shared status-values update, and release packet. The work remains a draft until the API owner confirms target-environment deployment.

Freeze the contract and examples

Read the approved operation contract, implementation behavior, integration tests, and version policy. Record that the old values guide is stale. Document required shipmentId and shipment:read permission. The approved tests show 200 for an authorized found shipment, 403 without permission, and 404 for a missing ID under the visibility rule. Leave timeout retry guidance open until the owner confirms it. The held example uses a fictional ID and only public fields. Remove a copied live token and internal hold_reason. Parse the JSON, check schema alignment, and run the fixture test.

Review client impact and publication state

A client with exhaustive status handling fails on held, while a client with an unknown-status fallback remains usable. The change therefore needs a migration note and coordinated release decision even though the response field remains a string. Update the shared values page and inspect links for semantic freshness, not only destination existence. Confirm that held is deployed in the target environment before the public page claims it is live. Keep the operation page, tests, migration note, deployment receipt, and editorial approval together for review.

GET /v2/shipments/{shipmentId}; permission shipment:read.
200 fixture: {"shipment_id":"SH-4721","status":"held"}.
403: missing permission; 404: missing visible ID.
No public hold_reason; no real token in examples.
Client check: exhaustive mapping may fail on new held value.
Release: update values page, test links/examples, confirm deployment.

Performance and operating cost

Reviewing E affected endpoints, C client integrations, L links, and X examples needs O(E+C+L+X) targeted checks before release. JSON parsing of an example is O(B) for B bytes; that syntax check does not prove authorization or compatibility. Keeping the evidence packet scoped to one operation reduces model context cost and review noise. A deployment receipt answers whether the service serves held; a merged code change and passing docs build do not. The editorial owner may hold publication when the schema, test, and running service disagree.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not publish an internal field or live credential.
  • Do not call an added enum value universally compatible.
  • Do not label staged behavior public before deployment is confirmed.

title: Infrastructure prompts: bind scope, owner, and environment
summary: Identify the exact managed resource, workspace, desired change, and forbidden effects.
body:
An infrastructure-change prompt is a review contract for a stateful system. It should name the environment, workspace, resource owner, desired configuration change, expected plan shape, and effects that must block progress. The prompt can draft configuration or inspect a sanitized plan, but it cannot infer that a repository directory points at the intended cloud account. Require the operator to verify the selected workspace and provider identity outside the model before planning. Separate a proposed edit from a reviewed plan and an applied change. Record the current value and target value so an attractive diff does not quietly expand scope to unrelated resources.

Operational case

A fictional Aster Reports team wants to change queue retention from 47 hours to 71 hours in its production workspace. The queue is managed by the reports platform team. A database in the same workspace is out of scope; any proposed database replacement blocks the change. The prompt asks for the queue address, workspace identity, current and target retention, owner, and expected in-place update. It leaves provider account and workspace confirmation to a trusted operator check. A model cannot establish that the terminal is in production merely because a folder is named prod.

Environment: Aster Reports production; operator verifies workspace/account.
Owned resource: report queue; retention 47h -> 71h.
Expected: one in-place retention update.
Blocked: database replacement, deletion, import, or address move.
Owner: reports platform team; apply requires reviewed plan and receipt.

Performance and operating cost

Inspecting R relevant managed resources is O(R) review work, while verifying the target workspace is a separate identity check. A narrow prompt reduces context size and makes an unexpected replacement easier to notice. A plan can contact provider APIs and may expose sensitive values, so a full raw state dump is not a cheap or safe substitute for a targeted summary. Require a human to confirm the environment before any operation that could change remote state.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer account identity from a directory name.
  • Do not let an unrelated database replacement ride with a queue change.
  • Do not report configuration text as an applied infrastructure change.

title: Infrastructure plans: classify every action before apply
summary: Compare the actual plan with the approved change envelope and stop on replacement.
body:
A plan-review prompt should parse each proposed resource action into create, in-place update, replacement, destroy, import, or state-only change, then compare it with the approved envelope. Replacement is not merely a larger update; it may interrupt service or lose data even when the final name stays the same. Ask which attribute causes replacement and whether it is tied to the requested change. Unknown or sensitive plan fields remain unknown; do not guess at them from a provider's normal behavior. A speculative plan is useful evidence, but the final apply must use a fresh approved plan or a saved reviewed plan under the team's workflow.

Operational case

Aster's sanitized plan shows the expected queue-retention update and an unexpected production database replacement. The prompt lists both actions and blocks approval. It asks the operator to inspect the database change's cause and compare current configuration, provider version, and recent drift before any apply. The team later fixes the unintended attribute and regenerates a plan with only the queue update. The old blocked plan is kept in the review record, but it is not used for execution. A fluent summary saying 'minor retention change' would be false while the replacement remains in the plan.

Plan P1: queue retention update -> expected candidate.
Plan P1: database replacement -> BLOCK; cause unresolved.
Investigate configuration, provider, and drift; do not apply P1.
Plan P2: queue update only -> eligible for owner review.
Apply only the exact reviewed plan under the approved workflow.

Performance and operating cost

Classifying A plan actions is O(A) inspection before deeper dependency review. A single unexpected replacement can dominate risk, so average action counts are not enough; check every destructive or state-changing action individually. Replanning adds time and provider calls but prevents an obsolete plan from being treated as current evidence. A saved plan file can contain sensitive material and must be handled as a controlled artifact, not attached to public documentation or pasted into an unrestricted prompt.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not summarize a plan by its requested change while hiding extra actions.
  • Do not treat replacement as an in-place update.
  • Do not approve a new plan merely because an earlier plan was reviewed.

title: Infrastructure prompts: quarantine state secrets and drift
summary: Use redacted evidence to separate manual drift from intended configuration changes.
body:
Infrastructure state and plan files may contain credentials, identifiers, and other sensitive attributes. A prompt should receive only the fields needed for the current question, with secrets and unrelated resources removed. Redaction must preserve action type and the attribute path that explains a proposed change; otherwise the model may call a dangerous replacement harmless. Drift is a difference between recorded configuration or state and observed infrastructure, not automatic permission to overwrite the live value. The prompt should ask whether the manual change is intentional, who owns it, and whether the desired state should adopt or reverse it. State access and lock recovery belong to controlled operational tools, not model instructions.

Operational case

Aster's database replacement is traced to a manual setting change made during an earlier incident, while the queue-retention request is unrelated. The prompt receives a redacted attribute diff and incident change record, not the full state file. It marks the database question as a separate ownership decision: keep the manual value and update configuration, or revert it through an approved change. Until that is resolved, the queue plan must be regenerated without an accidental database action. A hidden token in the state is never needed to classify the replacement, so it remains outside the model context.

Input: resource address, action, changed attribute name, redacted values.
Drift: database manual setting changed during prior incident.
Unknown: whether to adopt or reverse; owner must decide.
Never paste raw state, token, or saved binary plan into the prompt.
Regenerate and review the queue-only plan after resolution.

Performance and operating cost

Redacting N plan fields is O(N) work; manual review is still needed for fields whose names reveal sensitive information. A narrow diff lowers model token use and disclosure risk. Drift investigation may require a separate incident record and owner conversation, which costs more than simply applying the plan but preserves change authority. If a state lock is held, diagnose its active owner before recovery; deleting a lock based on a model guess can allow concurrent writes and corrupt the operational record.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not paste raw state into a general-purpose prompt.
  • Do not treat detected drift as approval to overwrite an incident change.
  • Do not force-unlock state without establishing whether another run is active.

title: Infrastructure apply: separate review from execution
summary: Require a reviewed plan identity, authorized operator, lock, and apply receipt.
body:
An apply prompt may prepare an execution checklist, but approval and execution are separate capabilities. The checklist should identify the reviewed plan, target workspace, authorized operator, change window, state lock, expected actions, and stop conditions. Verify that the plan applied is the one reviewed or that a newly generated plan received fresh approval. Do not issue an auto-approve command just because the prompt says 'safe.' After apply, collect the tool's outcome, changed resource identities, and any partial failure. A model assertion that apply succeeded is not a receipt. If execution fails midway, inspect live state before deciding whether to retry or rollback.

Operational case

After Aster resolves the unrelated database drift, plan P2 contains only the 47-to-71-hour queue-retention update. The reports platform owner approves P2 for the verified production workspace. The operator checks that no other run holds the state lock, executes the reviewed plan through the controlled pipeline, and records run R-47. The pipeline reports the queue update completed, but the team still checks the queue's actual retention setting and a new plan for unexpected changes. If P2 had changed since review, the approval would not transfer automatically. The prompt can list these checks; it cannot click apply or declare success from its own prose.

Reviewed plan: P2; queue retention update only.
Target: verified production workspace and account.
Authority: reports platform owner approves; operator executes.
Receipt: pipeline run R-47 with action result and timestamp.
Postcheck: live queue setting 71h; no unexpected plan actions.

Performance and operating cost

The checklist is O(A) for A reviewed actions, with extra time for locking, identity checks, and post-apply verification. A saved plan avoids silently applying a different set of proposed changes, but the artifact needs restricted storage because it may contain secrets. Postchecks are not redundant: provider completion can precede application-level readiness or reveal partial execution. Maintain a rollback or forward-fix route appropriate to the resource; changing retention back may not restore messages that already expired under an earlier policy.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not confuse a plan approval with permission for any later plan.
  • Do not call a model summary an apply receipt.
  • Do not assume a failed apply left every resource unchanged.

title: Infrastructure release: verify live state and rollback limits
summary: Check the actual resource, drift, behavior, and recovery path after apply.
body:
An infrastructure release prompt should state what must be true after apply and how each claim will be checked. Compare the live resource, a fresh plan, application behavior, and relevant monitoring with the approved change. A zero-diff plan alone may miss a user-visible failure, while a healthy dashboard cannot prove the desired configuration was applied. Define rollback or forward-fix conditions before release and name the owner who can act. Some changes are not fully reversible: reducing retention later will not recreate events already deleted. The release packet should preserve plan identity, apply receipt, observed state, tests, and unresolved limits.

Operational case

For Aster, pipeline run R-47 reports the queue setting changed from 47 to 71 hours. A direct provider read confirms 71 hours; a fresh plan has no unexpected actions. The reports team checks that new messages are accepted and an existing test message remains readable. Operations watches queue age and dead-letter count during the observation window. A rollback plan can restore the configured retention value, but cannot guarantee recovery of a message that expired before the change. The reviewer records the earlier blocked database replacement as resolved separately rather than pretending it never occurred.

Receipt: R-47 applied P2 to verified production workspace.
State: provider read says 71h; fresh plan shows no unexpected action.
Behavior: message acceptance and retained test record pass.
Monitor: queue age, failed delivery, dead-letter count.
Limit: reverting retention cannot resurrect expired messages.

Performance and operating cost

For V postchecks across R relevant resources, review work is O(V+R), plus an observation period set by workload behavior. A fresh plan and provider read add calls but test different failure modes. Track the tested time window: a five-minute smoke test cannot establish long-term retention behavior by itself. A small controlled fixture can verify that the service still accepts and reads messages now, while retention outcomes need later observation or a safe accelerated test environment.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer application health solely from a zero-diff infrastructure plan.
  • Do not promise rollback can restore already expired data.
  • Do not close the change without checking the actual resource and operator receipt.
