title: Terminal agents: request only the missing execution scope
summary: Describe a blocked operation precisely and preserve work that can continue locally.
body:
A terminal agent may run in a sandbox that grants selected reads, writes, and network calls. A permission failure is evidence about the environment, not a signal to bypass it with another tool or path. Identify the exact operation, target, and reason it is needed; then request the narrow capability through the approved mechanism when the user's task calls for it. Keep independent work moving while the request is pending. A shell command that reads a protected file is still a protected read even if the ordinary file tool denied it. Prompts cannot turn an operating-system boundary into authorization.

Operational case

Manifest Gate's importer and tests are inside the writable checkout, so the agent can implement and validate the duplicate-slug fix locally. A later integration check needs a staging endpoint outside the sandbox network policy. The agent records the blocked endpoint and the purpose of the check, then completes local tests and a reviewable patch. It does not route through an unrelated browser session to evade the block. If access is not granted, the final report marks staging verification as incomplete without downgrading the local evidence.

Allowed: edit importer and run local tests.
Blocked: staging endpoint request denied by network policy.
Request: access to the exact staging check, with purpose.
Meanwhile: finish local validation and diff review.
No access: report staging result as unverified.

Performance and operating cost

A denied operation can add waiting time, but repeated equivalent probes consume time without changing the permission state. Scope requests to the single missing resource rather than broad filesystem or network access. Recording the denial and local checks is O(1) per attempt plus the cost of those checks. A test omitted for environmental reasons must remain visible in the release packet.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a sandbox denial as permission to try a side channel.
  • Do not ask for broad access when one endpoint or path is enough.
  • Do not silently label an unrun integration check as passed.

title: Terminal agents: keep the patch within owned files
summary: Compare before and after state, preserve unrelated edits, and stop on ownership conflicts.
body:
A patch plan should name the files and behavior it intends to change. Before editing, capture the current diff and identify pre-existing changes. After editing, inspect the new diff and explain every changed file against the request. Avoid broad formatting passes that rewrite unrelated code merely to make the patch look consistent. If another agent or person changes the same file during work, re-read it and merge intent deliberately; never restore a stale copy over their work. The prompt may propose a minimal patch, but the filesystem and version-control checks establish what actually changed.

Operational case

The Manifest Gate task touches importer validation and its focused tests. An existing stylesheet edit belongs to another task. The agent changes only the importer and test fixture, then compares the final diff with the starting state. A background process updates the import schema while the agent is working; the agent rereads that schema before finalizing its validation call. It does not revert the concurrent update. If the schema change makes the original approach invalid, the agent adjusts the patch and reruns affected checks.

Owned: importer validation and importer tests.
Pre-existing: stylesheet edit; preserve it.
Concurrent: schema update; reread before final patch.
Review: every new changed file maps to duplicate-slug request.
Conflict: adapt and retest; never overwrite stale state.

Performance and operating cost

A diff review is O(D) in changed lines, far cheaper than scanning an entire repository after every small edit. Re-reading a contested file costs O(F) for its content size and prevents accidental loss of another change. A minimal patch usually shortens code review and rollback, but do not omit a necessary migration or fixture update solely to minimize line count. Ownership is a correctness constraint, not a cosmetic preference.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not erase unrelated work to obtain a clean diff.
  • Do not run a repository-wide formatter for a two-file fix without need.
  • Do not apply a stale patch after another writer changed the same file.

title: Terminal agents: make the final claim match verified checks
summary: Tie reported behavior to the exact tests, build, and remaining limits.
body:
A terminal workflow ends with a claim about the resulting state, not with the last command typed. Check the targeted behavior, run the repository's required checks, inspect the final diff, and confirm that generated artifacts correspond to the edited code. Report what passed, what failed, what was not run, and why. A test that mirrors the implementation can pass while the user contract remains broken; include an independent acceptance case. A green build does not prove a deployment occurred. If the environment blocks a check, state the limit and provide the evidence that is available.

Operational case

The importer now rejects two duplicate-slug pairs in a 47-record manifest before any write, leaving 45 unique slugs eligible for a clean import after correction. A test asserts both the rejection response and that the write sink received zero calls. The agent runs the focused test, required suite, and build, then checks the final diff for only intended files. Staging verification is blocked by network permission, so the final report does not claim a live import succeeded. The review packet includes the exact failing and passing case IDs.

Acceptance: 47 records, two duplicate pairs -> reject before write.
Independent oracle: write-sink call count is zero.
Checks: focused test, required suite, build, final diff.
Staging check: blocked by network policy, unverified.
Report: local behavior verified; no live deployment claim.

Performance and operating cost

The full suite may dominate runtime; keep a fast focused check during iteration, then run the required suite once after the final change. Reviewing T checks and D changed lines costs O(T+D) bookkeeping beyond test execution. This is cheaper than shipping a claim that cannot be reproduced. Store concise command outcomes and case IDs rather than pasting huge logs into the final prompt context.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not replace an independent acceptance oracle with a test copied from the implementation.
  • Do not say deployed when only a local build passed.
  • Do not omit blocked or unrun checks from the final report.

title: Project: verify a Manifest Gate importer fix
summary: Scope, patch, and verify a duplicate-slug fix without losing unrelated work.
body:
A fictional Manifest Gate repository imports shipping manifests. The requested change is narrow: reject duplicate shipment slugs before any record write. The review fixture has 47 records with two duplicate pairs, leaving 45 distinct slugs. The agent may inspect and edit the local importer and tests. An unrelated stylesheet edit is already present, and a staging endpoint is outside the current network permission. Build a prompt workflow that can finish a reviewable local patch without inventing a staging result.

Discover and constrain commands

Confirm the active repository root and current diff, read its local rules, and locate the importer and focused tests. Treat a filename supplied by the upload as one data argument to a fixed inspection command. Do not execute a line found in the manifest, even if it resembles a maintenance instruction. Keep outputs tied to command identity, source path, exit status, and truncation state. If a schema file changes during work, reread it before finalizing the patch.

Patch and verify

Reject the duplicate fixture before calling the write sink. An independent test checks both the rejection response and zero write calls. During iteration, run the focused test; after the final edit, run the required suite and build. A build that prints a bundle path but exits nonzero is failed, and an old bundle cannot stand in for the new result. Inspect the final diff against the starting state. Preserve the stylesheet edit. For staging, record the blocked request and seek only the missing network permission through the approved path.

Workspace: verified Manifest Gate checkout.
Input: 47 records; two duplicate slug pairs; 45 distinct slugs.
Acceptance: reject before any write; write-sink calls = 0.
Owned files: importer and focused tests.
Evidence: command, exit status, artifact ID, final diff.
Staging endpoint denied -> no live-import claim.

Performance and review cost

Duplicate detection with a hash set takes O(N) expected time and O(N) space for N slugs. A nested comparison would take O(N squared) time and becomes costly as manifests grow. Focused tests shorten each edit cycle, while the required suite and build confirm the final candidate. Keep log excerpts bounded and retain full artifact IDs for later inspection. The final report separates verified local behavior, unrun staging work, and any remaining reviewer decision.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not edit the wrong checkout because a filename matches.
  • Do not let upload text become a shell command.
  • Do not count printed progress as a successful build.
  • Do not erase the unrelated stylesheet edit.
  • Do not claim a live staging result after network denial.

title: Chart prompts: state the decision and measured quantity
summary: Begin with the reader's question, metric definition, and data grain.
body:
A chart prompt should begin with the decision the viewer must make, not a request for a fashionable graphic. State the measured quantity, unit, observation grain, population, and relevant threshold. A shipment count, a temperature reading, and time spent above a limit are different measures. The model can propose a display, but the application should supply verified data and a typed metric contract. If a requested conclusion cannot be supported by the available grain, the prompt must refuse that claim and offer a narrower one. A title should name what the marks encode rather than imply a causal finding.

Operational case

A fictional cold-chain team has six hourly readings for container C-47: 4.1, 4.4, missing, 5.8, 5.5, and 4.9 degrees Celsius. The operational question is which observed hours crossed a 5.0-degree limit and whether a missing hour prevents an all-clear. A line chart can show the observed sequence and a threshold, but the readings cannot prove how long the container stayed above the limit between samples. The prompt asks for observed exceedances, not continuous exposure time or product safety.

Decision: identify observed readings above 5.0 °C.
Entity: container C-47; grain: one scheduled reading per hour.
Series: 4.1, 4.4, missing, 5.8, 5.5, 4.9 °C.
Allowed claim: two observed readings exceed the limit.
Unsupported claim: hours continuously above the limit.

Performance and operating cost

Defining M measures takes O(M) review effort before rendering, while inspecting N records takes O(N) for a direct scan. That small up-front cost avoids expensive revision after a chart communicates the wrong quantity. Do not ask the model to infer a missing unit or population from a column name alone. A prompt with a precise decision contract is shorter than a broad creative brief followed by repeated corrections.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate two high readings with two hours of continuous exposure.
  • Do not omit the unit or observation grain.
  • Do not write a safety conclusion that the readings cannot establish.

title: Chart prompts: choose marks and scales by data type
summary: Match time, categories, and magnitudes to an explicit visual encoding.
body:
A prompt for chart creation should map each field to a visual channel with a reason. Ordered time points can use positions along a time axis; independent categories can use bars or dots. The chosen mark should preserve the comparison the reader needs. State the scale domain and whether zero is required for a magnitude comparison. A truncated bar axis can exaggerate a small difference; a nonzero line-axis baseline may be acceptable when clearly labeled and used to inspect small variation. Avoid dual axes unless their units and relationship are explicit. Color should carry a named category or status, not decorate the page.

Operational case

Container C-47's hourly readings are ordered observations. The chart uses points connected only across adjacent observed hours. It places time on the horizontal axis, degrees Celsius on the vertical axis, and a labeled 5.0-degree threshold. The missing third hour breaks the connection; no line segment crosses that gap. A separate category comparison of depot counts would use bars with a zero baseline. The prompt does not request a pie chart for hourly values or a second axis for an unrelated humidity series.

Mark: point plus line for adjacent observed readings.
X: scheduled hour in local time; Y: temperature in °C.
Threshold: labeled 5.0 °C reference line.
Missing hour: visible gap, not an interpolated mark.
No dual axis and no unlabelled scale truncation.

Performance and operating cost

Rendering N marks is generally O(N), while adding too many series increases visual search and legend review. A long sequence may need downsampling, but the method must preserve peaks relevant to the threshold. Encoding review is a low-cost gate: inspect whether the field type, unit, baseline, and mark agree before drawing. If the model invents a chart type first and maps data afterward, a misleading scale can survive even when every underlying value is correct.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not join points across a missing interval.
  • Do not use a nonzero bar baseline for an ordinary magnitude comparison.
  • Do not encode an unlabelled second unit on the same axis.

title: Chart prompts: expose missing data and checked denominators
summary: Keep absent observations distinct from zero and compute rates over eligible records.
body:
A chart prompt must state how missing, invalid, duplicate, and late records affect both marks and summary statistics. A missing temperature is not a zero-degree reading. Count eligible observations separately from scheduled slots, then name the denominator whenever a rate appears. Do not interpolate missing values unless the task explicitly authorizes a method and labels the result as estimated. When duplicate readings conflict, resolve the data issue before plotting rather than letting the model choose a convenient value. A chart can show uncertainty or a gap; it need not manufacture a continuous series.

Operational case

C-47 has six scheduled slots and five valid observations. Two observed values exceed 5.0 degrees, so the observed exceedance rate is 2 divided by 5, or 40%; the missing slot is excluded from that denominator and remains visible as missing. The team does not call 40% the fraction of time above the limit. If the missing slot later receives a verified late reading, the chart version changes and the rate is recomputed. A conflicting duplicate at the same hour blocks release until the sensor record is reconciled.

Scheduled slots: 6; valid readings: 5; missing: 1.
Observed exceedances: 2; eligible denominator: 5.
Observed exceedance rate: 2 / 5 = 40%.
Missing slot: gap, not 0 °C.
Conflicting duplicate: hold chart until resolved.

Performance and operating cost

A single pass over N records can validate slot membership and compute counts in O(N) time with O(U) storage for U unique slot keys. Reconciliation of duplicates may add review time, but it prevents a false aggregate from being repeated in reports. Displaying the denominator adds little space and removes ambiguity. Keep rate and count together so a viewer does not mistake a small sample for a stable operational trend.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not plot a missing reading as zero.
  • Do not divide by six when the stated rate is over five valid observations.
  • Do not describe a reading fraction as elapsed exposure time.

title: Chart prompts: produce a reproducible spec and data lineage
summary: Store field mappings, transforms, inputs, and version IDs outside prose.
body:
A chart-generation prompt should produce a machine-checkable spec, not only a picture and a persuasive caption. The spec records the input dataset version, field names and types, filters, aggregations, scale domains, threshold, missing-value rule, and output size. Keep raw data and transforms separate so a reviewer can recompute every mark. A rendered image is a view of that spec; it is not evidence that the transformation was correct. The application validates the spec against an allowlist of fields and operators before rendering. Store a content hash or immutable artifact ID for the exact input used.

Operational case

The C-47 chart packet names snapshot S-47 and a six-slot window. Its spec maps local hour to x, observed temperature to y, and a 5.0-degree threshold to a reference line. It rejects a model-proposed field called estimated_temperature because that field is not in the approved dataset. A late third-hour record later creates snapshot S-48 and a new chart version; the old report remains tied to S-47. The reviewer can compare the two versions without asking the model to remember how it drew the first one.

Input: snapshot S-47, six scheduled slots.
Fields: local_hour, observed_temperature_c, reading_status.
Transform: valid readings only for rate; missing slot retained as gap.
Encoding: hour -> x; temperature -> y; limit -> rule.
Reject unknown field: estimated_temperature_c.

Performance and operating cost

Validating K spec fields and transforms is O(K), with a separate O(N) check against N source rows when recomputing marks. Storing one compact spec per version is inexpensive relative to keeping an unreviewable screenshot as the only artifact. A renderer can change appearance across releases, so preserve both spec version and rendered output ID when comparing. The prompt should not bury important transforms in free-form wording that a parser cannot verify.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not accept a field the approved dataset does not contain.
  • Do not replace source data lineage with a screenshot filename.
  • Do not silently mutate an old chart when a late record arrives.

title: Chart prompts: review rendered and nonvisual outputs
summary: Check the image, labels, text alternative, and underlying values as one artifact.
body:
A valid chart spec does not guarantee a readable result. Review the rendered artifact at its intended size, including axis labels, units, threshold annotation, legend, contrast, and clipping. Provide a concise text alternative that states the chart's purpose and a longer data view when exact values matter. Avoid encoding status by color alone; pair it with labels or distinct marks. The text alternative must match the actual plot, including missing intervals and uncertainty, rather than repeating an earlier draft claim. A release gate compares rendered marks with the source table and checks keyboard or screen-reader access when the chart is interactive.

Operational case

The C-47 plot renders correctly at desktop width but clips the 5.0-degree threshold label on a narrow report page. A visual review catches the cut-off label before release. The text alternative states that two of five observed hourly readings exceed the limit and that the third scheduled hour is missing. An accompanying data view lists all six slots, including the missing one. The team checks that an interactive tooltip is reachable by keyboard; if it is not, the static data view still exposes the exact values.

Visual check: title, time zone, °C axis, 5.0 °C label, gap.
Text: two of five observed readings above limit; one missing slot.
Exact data: six scheduled rows available in a data view.
Color: supplemented by labels or distinct marks.
Narrow render: threshold label must remain visible.

Performance and operating cost

A visual review costs a small fixed inspection per viewport, while exact value reconciliation requires O(N) comparisons for N plotted rows. Accessible alternatives add authoring time but allow a reader to obtain the same critical finding without relying on color or pixels. Automated schema checks cannot catch clipping, misleading label placement, or a stale text alternative. Treat the rendered chart and its nonvisual description as one release unit.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume a valid spec means the rendered chart is legible.
  • Do not make color the sole carrier of threshold status.
  • Do not publish a text alternative that ignores the missing hour.

title: Project: review a cold-chain temperature chart
summary: Create and verify an evidence-bound hourly temperature chart.
body:
Prepare a prompt and review packet for a fictional cold-chain container C-47. Six hourly slots contain five observed temperatures in degrees Celsius: 4.1, 4.4, a missing third slot, 5.8, 5.5, and 4.9. The limit is 5.0. The reader needs to see which observed values exceed that limit and where the record is incomplete. The project creates a chart contract and a review plan; it does not assert product safety or infer continuous exposure between samples.

Build the chart contract

Use ordered hourly points, a labeled temperature axis, and a labeled limit line. Break the line at the missing third slot. The observed exceedance rate is two of five valid readings, or 40%, with the denominator printed beside the rate. The prompt must reject a zero substituted for the missing slot and must not claim two hours continuously above the threshold. A late verified reading changes the dataset version and triggers a new chart, rather than overwriting the original report.

Review the artifact

Bind the chart to snapshot S-47 and list the exact fields and transforms. Validate that every requested field exists and that the rendered marks match the six-slot data view. Inspect desktop and narrow layouts for labels, clipping, and a visible gap. Provide a text alternative that states two of five observed readings exceed the limit and one slot is missing. If an interactive tooltip is not keyboard accessible, the exact data view must still carry the values.

C-47 slots: 4.1, 4.4, missing, 5.8, 5.5, 4.9 °C.
Limit: 5.0 °C; observed exceedances: 2 / 5 = 40%.
Chart: hourly points, gap at slot 3, labeled limit line.
Packet: snapshot S-47, field mapping, transform, render ID.
Claim boundary: no continuous-exposure or safety conclusion.

Performance and review cost

A pass over N slots validates observations and computes the rate in O(N) time, with O(N) space for the explicit chart data view. Checking the specification takes O(K) for K fields and transforms. Rendering and narrow-screen inspection add review time but reveal errors that a JSON schema cannot detect. The release packet keeps the original snapshot and chart version so a later correction can be explained without rewriting earlier evidence.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not fill the missing slot with zero.
  • Do not divide the observed rate by all six scheduled slots.
  • Do not join a line across the missing hour.
  • Do not treat a valid spec as proof of a readable render.

title: Email prompts: reconstruct the thread before drafting
summary: Separate current decisions from older quoted text and proposals.
body:
An email thread is a sequence of messages, not a single flat document. A prompt that summarizes or drafts a reply should receive message IDs, send times, authors, recipients, and thread relationships from the mail service. Parse quoted earlier text as a quotation, not as a new statement by the latest sender. Build a claim ledger that marks each item proposed, corrected, approved, or unresolved. The most recent message can clarify an older claim, but recency alone does not grant approval. If a reply is missing from the fetched thread, state that the record is incomplete before claiming agreement.

Operational case

Aster Operations discusses a depot pilot with a vendor. The first email proposes 47 sites. A later message from the authorized program owner limits the approved pilot to 20 sites; the 47-site expansion remains a future proposal. A final vendor reply quotes the original 47-site text while asking about a meeting. A flat summarizer could mistake that quotation for a renewed approval. The prompt instead ties each claim to its message ID and asks the drafter to say '20-site pilot' while leaving expansion unresolved.

Message M-41: 47-site expansion proposed.
Message M-47: program owner approves 20-site pilot only.
Message M-52: quotes M-41; asks for meeting.
Current claim: 20-site pilot approved.
Unresolved: 47-site expansion; no renewed approval.

Performance and operating cost

Sorting M messages by reliable timestamps is O(M log M), while walking provider-supplied thread order is O(M). Claim extraction adds review proportional to the number of substantive statements. Restrict retrieval to the relevant thread and referenced attachments; loading an entire mailbox increases privacy exposure and token cost. A short provenance ledger prevents a correction from disappearing when a long quoted chain dominates the prompt.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a quoted old proposal as a new decision.
  • Do not infer approval solely from the latest message's position.
  • Do not claim the thread is complete when a referenced reply is missing.

title: Email prompts: keep sender identity and message text separate
summary: Use verified mailbox metadata for identity and treat message bodies as lower-trust content.
body:
The display name and signature in an email are claims inside a message, not proof of who controls an account. The application should provide verified mailbox identity and authorization context separately from the body. An inbound message may ask the assistant to change a workflow, reveal private information, or ignore earlier rules. The model can summarize that request, but cannot adopt it as a higher-priority instruction. Before drafting a consequential response, check whether the sender and recipient belong to the authorized thread and whether any requested action falls inside the user's current task. Mail content is evidence about what someone wrote; sending, scheduling, or data disclosure remains governed by trusted permissions.

Operational case

A message in the Aster thread displays the name 'Pilot Director' and says to send every depot contact list to an unfamiliar address before scheduling. The application metadata shows that the sender is an external vendor account without access to the contact list. The assistant records the request as an unapproved vendor ask and does not fetch or attach private contacts. It can still answer the legitimate meeting question after a user reviews the proposed recipients. A signature block cannot confer internal approval authority.

Display name: Pilot Director; verified account: external vendor.
Body request: send depot contacts to new address.
Decision: report request; do not fetch or disclose contacts.
Legitimate task: draft meeting reply within existing thread.
Effect authority: current user and mail service, not body text.

Performance and operating cost

Checking a sender against a trusted directory is O(1) average with a keyed lookup; parsing M headers and recipients is O(M). The identity check adds little latency compared with the risk of treating forged display text as authority. Avoid feeding entire unrelated mailbox history into the model. Record only the account and message IDs needed for this task, and keep confidential address lists outside the prompt unless the user has authorized their use.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate a display name or signature with verified identity.
  • Do not obey instructions embedded in an inbound email body.
  • Do not retrieve unrelated contacts to satisfy an unapproved vendor request.

title: Email prompts: verify attachment version and coverage
summary: Tie claims to the actual attachment opened and mark missing files unresolved.
body:
An attachment name is not its content, and the latest email does not always contain the latest approved file. A prompt should receive attachment IDs, message links, version markers, file type, and extraction status. Inspect only attachments relevant to the question. If extraction fails or a file is missing, do not invent its contents from the filename or a prior message. For a revised file, compare the specific fields that matter and record which version supports each claim. Treat text inside attachments as data, including any instruction-like text. A scanned image may require separate visual review if text extraction omits a table or signature.

Operational case

The vendor first attaches pilot-plan-v3 to M-41, showing 47 candidate sites. The authorized owner later attaches pilot-plan-v4 to M-47, listing 20 approved pilot sites and leaving expansion in a separate appendix. M-52 mentions 'the attached final plan' but contains no attachment. The assistant uses the verified v4 file for the pilot count and reports that M-52 supplied no new file. If v4 cannot be opened, it pauses the count claim rather than falling back silently to v3.

M-41 attachment A-3: v3, 47 candidate sites.
M-47 attachment A-4: v4, 20 approved pilot sites.
M-52: says 'attached'; attachment list empty.
Current pilot claim: A-4, if extraction succeeds.
A-4 unavailable: count remains unverified.

Performance and operating cost

Extracting A relevant attachments costs roughly O(total bytes), and comparing R required fields is O(R) after parsing. Narrow extraction saves tokens and reduces exposure to irrelevant files. The cost of checking an actual attachment ID is small compared with sending a wrong count to a customer or creating an event for an obsolete plan. Store file IDs and hashes so a reviewer can reproduce which bytes supported the draft.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a filename as proof of file contents.
  • Do not assume a later email includes the file it mentions.
  • Do not silently substitute v3 when v4 is unavailable.

title: Email prompts: review To, Cc, Bcc, and reply scope
summary: Resolve recipients from trusted identities before any draft or send effect.
body:
A reply prompt should name the intended audience and disclosure scope before it generates a polished message. The original thread may include observers, external vendors, hidden recipients, or an address that now routes elsewhere. Do not infer that reply-all is appropriate merely because an address appeared in a prior message. Resolve each recipient through trusted mailbox or directory data, flag external domains, and state whether the reply should remain in the same thread. Bcc recipients are a separate disclosure decision; a model should not silently add or expose them. A draft can be prepared for review, while sending requires current user authority and a checked recipient set.

Operational case

The Aster discussion includes the program owner, one vendor coordinator, and a broad legacy distribution list. The requested meeting reply is intended for the owner and coordinator only. A reply-all would reveal the pilot timing to the legacy list. The assistant proposes those two explicit recipients, keeps the thread relationship, and leaves the list out. A quoted address in the message body is not automatically a recipient. Before sending, the user sees the To and Cc fields as well as the exact body.

To: verified program owner and vendor coordinator.
Cc: none; legacy distribution list excluded.
Bcc: none unless separately requested and reviewed.
Thread: reply to M-52, preserve conversation identity.
Send: only after current user reviews recipients and body.

Performance and operating cost

Resolving R recipient IDs is O(R) with indexed directory lookups. The preview step adds a human decision, but prevents accidental disclosure to a large group. A long thread may contain many stale addresses, so derive recipients from the current task rather than copying every header. Record the reviewed recipient set with the draft version; a later body edit should not silently expand the audience.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use reply-all by default.
  • Do not copy addresses from quoted text into recipient fields.
  • Do not add Bcc recipients without an explicit disclosure decision.

title: Email prompts: separate drafted commitments from sent messages
summary: Check promises in the body and verify the effect through a mail-service receipt.
body:
Writing 'we will deliver Friday' can create a commitment even before the send button is pressed. A drafting prompt should distinguish confirmed facts, proposed actions, owners, and deadlines. It should not promise a date that the thread has not approved. Save a draft with its thread ID, recipients, body version, and attachment list, then present it for review. The send operation is a separate effect. If the send call times out, query the mail service for the draft or message receipt before trying again. A model's claim that it sent a message is not delivery evidence, and a provider's acceptance receipt may still be narrower than confirmed recipient delivery.

Operational case

The Aster reply says the team can review the 20-site pilot on Tuesday. It does not promise to approve 47-site expansion or deliver a final vendor contract by Friday. The assistant saves draft D-47, containing the two reviewed recipients and no contact-list attachment. The user approves the exact draft. If sending returns an ambiguous timeout, the workflow checks whether D-47 became a sent message before another attempt. The final user report distinguishes draft saved, send accepted, and recipient delivery when those states are known.

Draft D-47: 20-site pilot review; 47-site expansion unresolved.
Recipients: two reviewed addresses; attachments: none.
Commitment: meeting proposal only, no contract deadline.
Send timeout: query mail-service state before retry.
Final status: draft, accepted send, or confirmed delivery separately.

Performance and operating cost

A keyed receipt lookup is O(1) average; reviewing C commitment claims is O(C). An extra receipt query is cheaper than a duplicate email to an external party. Keep a stable draft ID and body version through retries. If the body or recipients change after approval, require a new review instead of treating the old approval as transferable. Measure drafting latency separately from mail delivery latency.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not write an unapproved deadline as a firm promise.
  • Do not call a saved draft a sent message.
  • Do not resend after an ambiguous timeout without checking mail-service state.

title: Calendar prompts: resolve availability, zone, and duration
summary: Turn a vague meeting request into a concrete interval before drafting an invite.
body:
A calendar prompt should request a date, start time, duration, named time zone, required attendees, and availability window. A local clock time without a zone can refer to several different instants. The application should convert proposed local times into resolved instants using its time-zone data and query free/busy for the calendars the user is allowed to inspect. Free/busy does not reveal the contents of private events; the assistant should not request those details unless authorized. A suggestion is not a confirmed booking. Check buffers, holidays, and the difference between a tentative hold and a final invite.

Operational case

The Aster vendor asks for 'Tuesday at 11:30' without naming a time zone. The assistant does not guess from the vendor signature. The program owner instead proposes Tuesday 15:00 to 15:45 UTC for three named attendees. The application checks each required calendar's availability for that exact interval and returns only free/busy status. One attendee has a conflict, so the assistant offers another verified slot rather than creating a conflicting invite. A 45-minute duration is explicit, not inferred from a default calendar setting.

Ambiguous request: Tuesday 11:30, zone missing -> clarify.
Owner proposal: Tuesday 15:00–15:45 UTC.
Required attendees: three verified identities.
Free/busy check: conflict found -> propose another checked slot.
No calendar effect before exact interval review.

Performance and operating cost

Checking A attendees across S candidate slots is O(AS) availability queries without batching; provider batch calls can reduce network overhead but not the logical checks. Time-zone conversion is inexpensive, yet a wrong instant can waste every attendee's time. Keep only free/busy results in the prompt when event titles are not needed. Recheck availability immediately before creating the event because calendars can change between suggestion and approval.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer a time zone from a signature or locale.
  • Do not treat a suggested time as a booked event.
  • Do not expose private event details when free/busy is sufficient.

title: Calendar prompts: distinguish create, update, and cancellation
summary: Bind every event change to an event ID, current state, guest list, and receipt.
body:
A calendar event is an external effect with an identity. Before creating one, review title, start and end instants, time zone, organizer, attendee list, location, and notification behavior. After creation, keep the returned event ID and version. A later request to move a meeting should update that event rather than create a near-duplicate. Read current state before applying a change, especially when another organizer may have edited it. Cancellation is distinct from deleting a local hold. If the API response is ambiguous, reconcile against the calendar by event ID and expected version before retrying. Prompt wording cannot substitute for the provider's effect receipt.

Operational case

After the Aster owner selects a conflict-free slot, the assistant prepares a 45-minute invite titled '20-site pilot review' for three checked attendees. The user reviews the details and authorizes creation. The calendar returns event E-47 and version V-1. The vendor later asks to move it by 30 minutes; the assistant checks E-47, recomputes the interval, reviews changed notifications, and updates the same event. If an update times out, it reads E-47 before sending another request. It does not create E-48 by assumption.

Proposed event: 20-site pilot review, 45 minutes, three attendees.
Create approved -> event E-47, version V-1.
Move request -> read E-47, check new interval, update E-47.
Timeout -> reconcile E-47 before retry.
Cancellation -> explicit scope and guest-notice review.

Performance and operating cost

A keyed event read is O(1) average at the application level, though network latency can dominate. Rechecking A attendee calendars adds O(A) logical availability checks per proposed change. Version matching and receipts add a small amount of state but prevent duplicate events and lost updates. Review notification behavior because editing an event can message guests even when the prompt describes the edit as minor.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not create a second event to move an existing one.
  • Do not assume a timeout means the create or update failed.
  • Do not cancel an entire event when the user meant one tentative hold.

title: Calendar prompts: scope recurrence changes to the right instances
summary: Separate one occurrence from an entire series and verify exceptions.
body:
A recurring meeting represents a rule plus individual occurrences and exceptions. A prompt should ask whether the user intends to edit one occurrence, this and later occurrences, or the whole series. Those scopes can produce different effects and guest notifications. Preserve the recurrence rule, time zone, exception dates, and organizer identity in the review packet. Do not infer a series-wide change from 'move next Tuesday.' A local display may show only a few generated occurrences, so check the underlying event identity before editing. After a change, inspect both the target occurrence and unaffected neighboring occurrences.

Operational case

Suppose the Aster pilot review becomes a weekly series for four weeks. The owner says 'move next Tuesday's call by 30 minutes.' The assistant targets only that dated occurrence and leaves the other three at their prior time. A separate later request to move all remaining sessions needs a new scope review. If one occurrence was cancelled, the assistant must not recreate it while updating the series. The calendar service returns exception or instance IDs that the application retains for verification.

Series: four weekly sessions, one named time zone.
Request: move next Tuesday only.
Target: dated instance, not whole recurrence rule.
Verify: target moved; other three unchanged.
Later series-wide request -> separate scope and notice review.

Performance and operating cost

Checking K generated occurrences and E exceptions is O(K+E) for a bounded review window. A series-wide update can affect many more guests and dates than a single-instance edit, so the prompt should present an effect count before approval. Avoid materializing an unbounded recurrence solely for a preview; choose a finite horizon and state it. A missing exception record can cause a cancelled meeting to reappear, so include cancellation cases in release tests.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not turn 'next Tuesday' into a change to every future meeting.
  • Do not lose a cancelled-instance exception during a series edit.
  • Do not claim an unbounded series was fully reviewed from a short preview.

title: Project: review an Aster vendor reply and invite
summary: Reconcile thread, attachments, recipients, and a tentative meeting interval.
body:
A fictional Aster Operations vendor thread begins with a 47-site expansion proposal. An authorized owner later approves only a 20-site pilot and attaches plan v4. A subsequent vendor message quotes the 47-site proposal and asks for a meeting, saying a final plan is attached even though the message has no attachment. The user wants a reply draft and a proposed calendar invite. This project creates a review packet; it does not send email or write a calendar event.

Resolve the thread and draft

Read message IDs, send times, verified account identities, recipients, and attachment lists. Use v4 to support the 20-site pilot count only if extraction succeeds. Treat the quoted 47-site text as an older proposal. The draft goes to the authorized owner and vendor coordinator, not the legacy distribution list. It proposes a pilot review and avoids promising a contract deadline. A new address requesting the depot contact list is an unapproved disclosure request, even if its display name claims seniority. Save the reviewed message as a draft with a stable ID.

Propose the calendar event

The vendor's 'Tuesday 11:30' lacks a time zone, so ask for clarification or use a separately confirmed interval. The owner supplies Tuesday 15:00–15:45 UTC. Check the three required attendees' free/busy state and recheck just before creating an event. If a conflict appears, offer a verified alternative. Creation, update, and cancellation each require a precise event identity and effect review. A later request to move one occurrence of a weekly series must not shift the whole series.

M-41: 47-site expansion proposed; attachment A-3 is v3.
M-47: 20-site pilot approved; attachment A-4 is v4.
M-52: quotes M-41; says attached but has no file.
Reply: two reviewed recipients; draft only; no contact list.
Invite candidate: Tuesday 15:00–15:45 UTC, three attendees.
Effects: send and create only after exact preview and current approval.

Performance and review cost

Thread reconstruction costs O(M log M) when M messages require timestamp ordering. Extract only the A attachments relevant to the decision, rather than the entire mailbox. Availability checks over S candidate slots and three attendees cost O(3S) logical queries. Receipt lookups add little relative to duplicate mail or calendar effects. The release suite tests a quoted old proposal, missing attachment, forged display name, reply-all disclosure, time-zone ambiguity, conflicting attendee, send timeout, event update timeout, and one-instance recurrence change.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not promote quoted expansion text to approval.
  • Do not invent the missing final attachment.
  • Do not send to the legacy list by default.
  • Do not guess the vendor's time zone.
  • Do not call a saved draft a sent message or a proposed time a booked event.

title: Location prompts: resolve ambiguous addresses before routing
summary: Separate user-entered address text from a verified stop identity.
body:
A location-aware prompt should not turn a free-text address into a route stop without validation. The application supplies candidate matches with address components, service area, match quality, and stable place identity. The prompt can compare candidates and ask a focused question, but a partial match or a nearby street is not the requested destination. Preserve the original address text next to the chosen candidate for review. A person's name or business label does not prove which entrance a vehicle can use. If the result is ambiguous, mark the stop unresolved and exclude it from a supposedly final route until a trusted user or authoritative record selects it.

Operational case

A fictional Quartz Field Service ticket lists '47 Harbor Lane, North Pier' for job J-47. The lookup returns two candidates: a full street-address match in North Pier and a partial match for Harbor Road in another district. The dispatcher selects the first candidate after checking the ticket's depot and entrance note. A different ticket says only 'Harbor Lane' and produces three plausible results; the assistant asks for a street number instead of choosing the nearest one. It keeps job IDs separate from map labels so a similar-looking address cannot silently become another customer's stop.

J-47 text: 47 Harbor Lane, North Pier.
Candidate P-47: full street match, correct service area.
Candidate P-71: partial street match, wrong district.
Decision: use P-47 after dispatcher review.
Unnumbered Harbor Lane ticket: unresolved, no final route.

Performance and operating cost

Checking C candidates per stop across S stops is O(SC) comparison work, usually small beside route computation. An extra clarification can delay dispatch, but routing to the wrong street can consume a whole service window. Keep candidate payloads narrow: the address components, match quality, and access point needed for the task. Do not copy unrelated place metadata or private customer notes into the prompt merely because a geocoder returned them.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a partial address match as verified destination identity.
  • Do not choose the nearest candidate merely because it is first.
  • Do not merge two jobs because their map labels look similar.

title: Location prompts: validate coordinates, units, and precision
summary: Check latitude-longitude order and avoid false precision in location claims.
body:
A coordinate pair needs a declared order, numeric range, coordinate system, and acquisition method. A prompt should not infer that the first number is latitude just because many examples use that order. A point may represent a building centroid rather than the service entrance, so an apparently precise map pin can still be operationally wrong. Store an accuracy or confidence field separately from the coordinate value. When a location is sensitive, pass only the precision necessary for the task and keep exact points out of public summaries. The application validates coordinate fields before they enter route calculations.

Operational case

Quartz receives a depot point in latitude-longitude order and an imported job point in longitude-latitude order. Both numeric values fall within legal global ranges, so a simple bounds check alone misses the swap. The import contract identifies each field name and coordinate system, and the application rejects the unlabeled pair. For J-47, the verified entrance point differs from the building centroid; the route uses the entrance. A manager-facing summary names the service area, while the exact customer location remains in the authorized dispatch tool.

Depot: latitude, longitude, declared coordinate system.
Imported J-47 pair: order missing -> reject until mapped.
J-47 route target: verified service entrance, not centroid.
Public summary: service area only.
Dispatch tool: exact point under access control.

Performance and operating cost

Validating N coordinate records is O(N). Detecting swapped-but-in-range values may require contextual checks against known service bounds or a sample review, adding O(N) comparisons. The extra metadata is tiny compared with an incorrect trip. Reduce precision only in outputs where exact location is unnecessary; do not round the operational route input so far that the driver loses the correct entrance.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assume coordinate order from unlabeled numbers.
  • Do not equate a building centroid with an approved entrance.
  • Do not expose exact customer coordinates in a broad status message.

title: Location prompts: label travel estimates and stale matrices
summary: Keep departure time, mode, and estimate source attached to each route leg.
body:
Travel time is an estimate for a particular origin, destination, mode, departure time, and routing preference. A prompt must not present a cached number as current traffic. The application should attach generation time, validity window, distance unit, and any fallback status to every route leg. If an element has no route or the provider used a fallback method, mark it for review rather than inventing a duration. For a multi-stop plan, retrieve the needed pairwise legs and check that all origins and destinations correspond to verified stop identities. The model can explain trade-offs but should not fabricate matrix cells.

Operational case

Quartz requests a driving matrix for three verified jobs and depot start at the planned morning departure. The result gives 22 minutes from depot to J-47, 18 minutes from J-47 to J-52, and 31 minutes from J-52 to J-71. A saved matrix from the previous week lists 16 minutes for the last leg; the prompt rejects that older cell for today's plan. If the current J-52 to J-71 element is missing, the route remains provisional even though the other two legs are available.

Mode: driving; departure: planned morning instant.
Fresh legs: depot→J-47 22 min; J-47→J-52 18 min.
Fresh leg: J-52→J-71 31 min.
Old J-52→J-71 value: 16 min -> do not substitute.
Missing current element -> provisional plan.

Performance and operating cost

A complete matrix for S stops can require O(S squared) origin-destination elements, while evaluating one fixed sequence needs only O(S) legs. Request only the combinations required by the planner and retain a matrix ID for review. Refreshing estimates adds network latency and possibly usage cost, but avoids a false on-time claim. A routing service may return estimates with uncertainty; the prompt should preserve that status instead of turning a prediction into a guaranteed arrival.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not present a week-old leg as current traffic.
  • Do not fill a missing matrix cell with an invented time.
  • Do not call an estimated arrival a guaranteed arrival.

title: Location prompts: compute stop-window feasibility before recommending
summary: Combine travel legs, service durations, and appointment windows with checked arithmetic.
body:
A route recommendation must satisfy more than short travel distance. For each stop, compute arrival from the previous departure and the selected travel estimate, then start service no earlier than the appointment window and finish within any hard end constraint. Preserve service duration, skill eligibility, capacity, break rules, and access restrictions as typed inputs. The prompt may rank feasible options, but a deterministic validator should reject routes with a missed hard window or missing leg. If a window is soft, label the trade-off explicitly; do not quietly reinterpret it as hard or vice versa.

Operational case

Technician T-8 leaves the Quartz depot at 08:30. A 22-minute leg reaches J-47 at 08:52; service waits until the 09:00 window and lasts 30 minutes, ending 09:30. An 18-minute leg reaches J-52 at 09:48; service starts 10:00 and ends 10:25 after 25 minutes. A 31-minute leg reaches J-71 at 10:56; service starts 11:00 and ends 11:20 after 20 minutes. Those calculations support the three stated windows, but only if the technician is eligible for all jobs and the travel estimates remain valid.

T-8 departs 08:30; depot→J-47 22 min; arrives 08:52.
J-47 window 09:00; service 30 min; departs 09:30.
J-52 arrival 09:48; starts 10:00; departs 10:25.
J-71 arrival 10:56; starts 11:00; finishes 11:20.
Release gate: skill, capacity, breaks, and access checked.

Performance and operating cost

Validating one ordered route of S stops is O(S) time and O(1) working state beyond the input. Searching every permutation is O(S factorial) and quickly impractical; use a route solver or bounded candidate set for larger fleets, then validate the chosen route independently. A few precise arithmetic checks prevent a fluent prompt from hiding a ten-minute conflict. Keep traffic estimates separate from appointment rules so a later refresh changes only the affected legs.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not add travel time without waiting for a window that has not opened.
  • Do not ignore service duration when checking the next stop.
  • Do not call a route feasible before skill and capacity rules are checked.

title: Location prompts: review the map and gate dispatch effects
summary: Check rendered stops and require current approval before sending a route.
body:
A route can pass arithmetic checks while its map points to the wrong entrance or omits a restricted road. The release packet should include ordered stop IDs, verified point identities, leg estimates, appointment windows, and a rendered map for human review. The map is a view of the route data, not proof that the points were correct. Before dispatching a change, recheck job status and technician availability; a completed or cancelled job must not remain in an active route. Sending the plan to a technician is an external effect with a recipient and receipt. If an update times out, reconcile the dispatch state before retrying.

Operational case

Quartz's plan for T-8 passes the three window calculations. The map preview reveals that J-52's marker sits at a loading dock closed to service vehicles, although the street address matches. The dispatcher substitutes the verified service entrance, refreshes affected travel legs, and reruns the feasibility check. Only after reviewing the updated route and the technician recipient does the user approve dispatch. A timeout after send triggers a receipt lookup; the assistant does not issue a second route simply because it cannot see the first response.

Review: ordered job IDs, entrance points, windows, leg IDs.
Map defect: J-52 marker at closed dock -> correct point.
Refresh changed legs and recompute arrivals.
Before send: job status and T-8 availability rechecked.
Send timeout: query dispatch receipt before retry.

Performance and operating cost

A map review adds a fixed human inspection plus O(S) stop checks for S route points. Recomputing only legs adjacent to a corrected stop is cheaper than rebuilding every candidate route, though global optimization may still be warranted if the correction changes feasibility. Receipt checks are O(1) average in a keyed store. The extra gates reduce wrong-address dispatches and duplicate technician instructions, both costlier than a short review.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a rendered map as validation of the original point identities.
  • Do not send a route that still contains a cancelled job.
  • Do not resend after an ambiguous dispatch timeout without checking the receipt.

title: Project: review a Quartz field-service route
summary: Check stop identity, current legs, window arithmetic, map points, and dispatch authority.
body:
Plan a fictional morning route for Quartz Field Service technician T-8. Three jobs have verified service entrances and fixed appointment windows. A fourth address is ambiguous and must remain outside the final candidate until the dispatcher confirms its street number. The task is to prepare a reviewable route recommendation, not to send directions. The prompt must keep address identity, coordinate order, travel estimates, service durations, and dispatch authority separate.

Validate locations and route inputs

For J-47, choose the full street-address match at 47 Harbor Lane after comparing it with a partial match in another district. Reject an imported coordinate pair whose order is not declared. Use the verified service entrance instead of a building centroid. The current driving matrix supplies 22 minutes from depot to J-47, 18 to J-52, and 31 to J-71 for the planned departure. A week-old 16-minute estimate for the last leg is not a substitute. A missing current leg leaves the plan provisional.

Compute and review

T-8 leaves at 08:30, reaches J-47 at 08:52, waits until 09:00, and finishes 30 minutes of service at 09:30. The next leg reaches J-52 at 09:48; its 10:00 start and 25-minute service end at 10:25. The final leg reaches J-71 at 10:56; a start at 11:00 and 20-minute service end at 11:20. Those times satisfy the stated windows only if skills, capacity, access, and break rules also pass. The map preview reveals a closed loading dock at J-52, so the dispatcher corrects the entrance and refreshes affected legs before approval.

J-47: 08:52 arrival; 09:00–09:30 service.
J-52: 09:48 arrival; 10:00–10:25 service.
J-71: 10:56 arrival; 11:00–11:20 service.
Ambiguous fourth address: excluded.
J-52 closed dock: correct point, refresh legs, recompute.
Dispatch: pending current user review and effect receipt.

Performance and operating cost

Validation of one ordered S-stop route is O(S), while a full pairwise travel matrix can grow as O(S squared). Searching every stop ordering grows factorially, so larger fleets need bounded candidates or a dedicated solver followed by independent validation. Map review and permission checks add time but expose errors that arithmetic cannot. The final packet includes place identities, matrix version, computed times, map artifact, recipient, and any dispatch receipt.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use the partial address match as a verified stop.
  • Do not guess coordinate order.
  • Do not replace a missing current leg with an old estimate.
  • Do not ignore waiting and service durations.
  • Do not send an unreconciled route after a timeout.

title: Interview prompts: limit transcript use to the study purpose
summary: Check permission and minimize participant detail before analysis.
body:
A research transcript is not a general-purpose prompt asset. Record the study question, permitted uses, retention boundary, participant identity key, and any excluded material before sending an excerpt to a model. Remove names, contact details, and incidental third-party stories unless they are needed for the analysis and permitted by the study. A prompt should refuse a request to repurpose interview text for outreach or a different study without a fresh authorization check. The application, not the prose instruction alone, decides which records the analyst may access. Use stable pseudonymous participant IDs so later coding can be traced without spreading direct identifiers.

Operational case

A fictional Parcel Window study has 12 volunteers discussing pickup-window selection. Interview P-07 mentions a neighbor's phone number while describing a delivery problem. The analyst keeps the pickup timing excerpt but removes that unrelated number before model review. The study permits aggregate product analysis; a marketing request to create a contact list from the transcripts falls outside that purpose. The prompt returns a purpose mismatch and records that no participant text was exported for the new request.

Study: Parcel Window pickup experience
Allowed: coded product findings from 12 interviews
P-07 excerpt: pickup window confusing; third-party number removed
Marketing contact extraction: purpose mismatch -> stop

Performance and review cost

Reviewing N excerpts for scope and identifying data takes O(N) passes, with a second human check for uncertain redactions. Keeping only needed segments lowers prompt size and exposure. The review is worth doing before analysis because a later summary cannot undo disclosure of an unnecessary phone number. Store the permission decision with the study record; never infer permission from the mere presence of a transcript file.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat access to a transcript as permission for every downstream use.
  • Do not leave incidental third-party identifiers in an analysis batch.
  • Do not let a prompt replace application-level access checks.

title: Interview prompts: preserve speaker and segment boundaries
summary: Keep each excerpt tied to a participant, question, and time span.
body:
Coding requires a stable unit of evidence. Split transcripts into segments that retain participant ID, speaker, interview question, time span, and a segment identifier. Keep enough surrounding turns to resolve pronouns and corrections, but do not join different participants into one fabricated quote. An automatic transcript may misassign a speaker or omit a negation; mark such spans uncertain and compare them with the recording when available. The model can propose segment boundaries, while the researcher resolves uncertain attribution. Each downstream code and finding should point back to the approved segment version.

Operational case

At 12:14, P-03 says a pickup window was 'fine' and immediately corrects that statement after describing a missed collection. A one-sentence clip would reverse the meaning. The analyst keeps the correction in segment P03-S18, records the time range, and marks a noisy word for audio review. P-08's later complaint about the same screen stays in its own segment; merging those two voices would falsely suggest one person described both events.

P03-S18 | speaker P-03 | 12:14-12:42
Initial: window was fine
Correction: collection missed after the window changed
Audio uncertainty: one word pending review
P08-S09: separate participant, separate segment

Performance and review cost

Segmenting T transcript turns is O(T) before any comparison between segments. Wider context improves interpretation but increases token cost, so attach nearby turns only where they change meaning. Versioning a corrected transcript adds storage but prevents a code from pointing at text that no longer exists. A model output without participant and segment keys is cheap to produce and expensive to audit.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not code the first sentence while dropping its immediate correction.
  • Do not merge similar remarks from different participants into one quote.
  • Do not silently repair uncertain speech without checking the recording.

title: Interview prompts: write a codebook with inclusion rules
summary: Define what qualifies for each code, including near misses.
body:
A code label is too vague to support consistent analysis. Give each code an operational definition, an inclusion test, an exclusion test, a representative excerpt, and a near miss. Let a segment hold more than one code when independent claims support them. Keep a version number for the codebook and distinguish new inductive candidates from approved codes. Ask the model for the segment ID, candidate code, evidence span, and reason; a researcher approves additions and ambiguous assignments. Do not interpret a broad word such as 'late' as a missed pickup if the speaker only describes a slow page.

Operational case

The Parcel Window team defines WINDOW_CLARITY for uncertainty about the pickup interval shown to the customer. P-07 says the app displayed 'morning' without an end time, so the segment qualifies. P-02 says the confirmation page loaded slowly but understood the interval; that is a near miss. An early model draft tags both as WINDOW_CLARITY. The researcher rejects the second assignment and adds a separate PAGE_LATENCY candidate only after checking the rest of the interviews.

Code WINDOW_CLARITY v2
Include: uncertain displayed pickup interval
Exclude: page delay with understood interval
P07-S11 -> include, missing end time
P02-S06 -> exclude; PAGE_LATENCY candidate

Performance and review cost

Applying K candidate codes to N segments can require O(NK) comparisons in a direct pass. A compact codebook reduces repeated interpretation but may miss a genuinely new pattern, so reserve a candidate-code lane and review it periodically. Version changes require recoding affected segments; the cost is explicit and preferable to mixing incompatible definitions in a single count.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use a label without an inclusion and exclusion test.
  • Do not force every new observation into an existing code.
  • Do not compare counts from different codebook versions without recoding.

title: Interview prompts: keep coder disagreement visible
summary: Record competing readings and resolve them against the segment.
body:
Two coders may read an interview segment differently for sound reasons. Capture each independent label, its supporting words, the codebook version, and the reason for disagreement before discussion. A model suggestion is another proposal, not an authoritative tie breaker. Adjudicate by checking the full segment and the code definition; if the evidence cannot settle the question, mark it unresolved and avoid a confident thematic claim. Report agreement only for an explicitly defined unit and label set. Do not turn a high agreement number into proof that the codes are meaningful or that the sample represents a wider population.

Operational case

Coder A marks P03-S18 as WINDOW_CLARITY because the revised time surprised the participant. Coder B marks it as NOTIFICATION_TIMING because the participant describes learning of the change too late. The full segment supports both mechanisms, so the review assigns two codes with separate evidence spans. Another unclear segment remains unresolved pending audio. The review log keeps the original assignments, the final decision, and who made it; a model does not erase the disagreement.

P03-S18 | codebook v2
Coder A: WINDOW_CLARITY | span 12:14-12:23
Coder B: NOTIFICATION_TIMING | span 12:25-12:42
Review: both codes, separate spans
P09-S04: unresolved until audio check

Performance and review cost

A second independent pass roughly doubles coding time for the reviewed subset, and adjudication grows with disputed segments D rather than every segment N. Sample a meaningful range of cases, including near misses, instead of only easy examples. The audit trail adds a small amount of storage and prevents silent consensus. It also reveals whether a codebook revision, rather than a different model prompt, is the right fix.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not let one model output overwrite independent coder decisions.
  • Do not force a single label when distinct supported mechanisms coexist.
  • Do not present unresolved segments as agreed evidence.

title: Interview prompts: build a theme evidence ledger
summary: Tie each proposed theme to segments, exclusions, and contrary cases.
body:
A theme is an interpretation across coded material, not a list of memorable quotes. For each candidate theme, maintain a claim, supporting participant-segment IDs, codebook version, the researcher’s interpretation, and counterexamples or boundaries. Ask the model to retrieve evidence for and against the candidate before drafting prose. If one statement is vivid but isolated, keep it as a case rather than saying the pattern recurred. A theme may include tension: some participants can value a wide pickup window while others need a narrow one. The finding must explain that variation instead of flattening it.

Operational case

The Parcel Window team proposes 'vague windows block planning.' Five of 12 participants describe an unclear interval, and two of those also explain why it affected a handoff. P-11 says the broad interval was useful because someone was always home; this contrary case belongs in the ledger. A first draft says 'everyone wanted exact times.' The evidence ledger rejects that wording and narrows the claim to planning problems among the five participants who raised it, with P-11 as a boundary case.

Theme: vague windows can impede pickup planning
Support: 5 participant IDs with verified segment links
Mechanism: 2 describe missed handoff planning
Counterexample: P-11 prefers a broad interval
Rejected claim: everyone wanted exact times

Performance and review cost

Building an index over N coded segments is O(N); checking a candidate theme against all relevant records is another O(N) scan unless indexed by code and participant. The scan is valuable because selective quote retrieval can hide a counterexample. Keep the ledger compact enough for a reviewer to open every cited span. An attractive paragraph without traceable supporting and contrary cases should not pass release.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a vivid isolated quote a recurring theme.
  • Do not hide participants whose accounts conflict with the proposed claim.
  • Do not treat a code name as the theme interpretation.

title: Interview prompts: count people, not repeated excerpts
summary: Keep the participant denominator separate from segment frequency.
body:
A single participant can mention the same problem several times. If the claim is about participants, deduplicate coded segments by participant ID before counting; if it is about mentions, say so and keep that separate measure. Preserve the eligible interview denominator, missing records, and recruitment scope. Qualitative interviews can show mechanisms and variation, but a small purposeful sample does not produce a population prevalence estimate. The prompt may compute descriptive counts from an explicit ledger, while a deterministic check reconciles those counts to distinct participant IDs.

Operational case

The Parcel Window ledger has 47 coded excerpts from 12 participants. Nine excerpts about window clarity come from five distinct participants; four of those excerpts are P-07 revisiting one event. Reporting '9 of 12 customers' would count text spans as people and overstate the finding. The study can say five of the 12 interviewed participants raised unclear windows, with the recruitment context nearby. Two participants mention a language barrier, but their remarks remain a separate finding rather than being folded into window clarity.

Eligible interviews: 12
Coded excerpts: 47
WINDOW_CLARITY excerpts: 9
Distinct WINDOW_CLARITY participants: 5
LANGUAGE_BARRIER participants: 2
Population prevalence: not estimated

Performance and review cost

Deduplicating M coded excerpts with a participant-ID set is O(M) expected time and O(P) memory for P distinct participants. Manual verification remains necessary for misassigned speakers and duplicated interview records. Descriptive counts are cheap; false precision is costly because it can make a narrow exploratory study look like a survey. Preserve both segment and participant counts so a reviewer can reproduce the statement.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not divide quote counts by participant counts.
  • Do not call 5 of 12 a population rate.
  • Do not combine separate codes merely to make a larger number.

title: Interview prompts: turn bounded findings into testable decisions
summary: State what the interviews support and what needs further testing.
body:
A research summary should separate observation, interpretation, design hypothesis, proposed action, and measurement plan. The model can draft a decision memo from an approved evidence ledger, but it should not present a product change as proven effective merely because participants described a problem. Attach every factual claim to participant-segment keys and every count to a reconciled denominator. Note whose experience is missing from the sample. A product owner can choose a reversible prototype, a usability test, or further recruitment, but the prompt must leave that decision and its trade-offs visible.

Operational case

Five interviewed participants describe ambiguous pickup windows; two describe a language barrier; P-11 prefers a flexible interval. The team proposes displaying both a plain-language range and an optional narrower alert, then testing comprehension and successful pickup planning with participants who have varied schedules and languages. The memo does not say that the design will reduce missed pickups. It says the interview evidence motivates the prototype and identifies what an experiment must measure before rollout.

Observed: 5 of 12 interviewees raised window clarity
Boundary: P-11 preferred flexibility
Hypothesis: explicit range plus optional alert aids planning
Next check: comprehension and pickup planning test
Rollout claim: withheld until measured

Performance and review cost

Drafting from indexed findings is O(F + E) for F findings and E cited evidence spans, but reviewer effort grows with the number of claims and contested excerpts. A short memo with open evidence links is cheaper to verify than a long narrative with hidden assumptions. Product testing adds time, yet it distinguishes a plausible remedy from a demonstrated one. Preserve a release record so later results do not silently rewrite what the interviews originally showed.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not describe a proposed feature as an observed improvement.
  • Do not remove the participant who challenges the preferred interpretation.
  • Do not make the model the final owner of the product decision.

title: Project: analyze Parcel Window pickup interviews
summary: Code a fictional pickup study, reconcile conflicting interpretations, and draft a bounded decision memo.
body:
Analyze a fictional Parcel Window study about choosing parcel pickup times. There are 12 consented interviews and 47 coded excerpts. The allowed use is aggregate product research. Build a reproducible, human-reviewed analysis from bounded transcript segments, not a contact list or a marketing audience. The deliverable is a decision memo with evidence links, disagreement records, counterexamples, and a testable next step.

Prepare and code the records

Remove an unrelated third-party phone number from P-07's transcript before model analysis. Keep P03-S18 as one contextual segment because P-03 corrects an initial claim; mark its noisy word for audio review. Use codebook v2: WINDOW_CLARITY includes uncertain displayed intervals and excludes a slow page when the interval was understood. Coder A and coder B assign different codes to P03-S18; the review keeps both WINDOW_CLARITY and NOTIFICATION_TIMING, each tied to its own span. P09-S04 stays unresolved until the recording is checked.

Reconcile themes and propose a check

Nine window-clarity excerpts come from five distinct participants, including four repeated mentions by P-07. Two participants report a language barrier. P-11 prefers a broad pickup interval; the counterexample stays beside the proposed theme. State 'five of the 12 interviewed participants' only as a sample description, not a population rate. Propose a plain-language range with an optional narrower alert. Test comprehension and pickup planning before claiming the feature improves outcomes.

Study: 12 interviews; 47 coded excerpts
WINDOW_CLARITY: 9 excerpts, 5 distinct participants
LANGUAGE_BARRIER: 2 distinct participants
Counterexample: P-11 prefers flexibility
P09-S04: unresolved audio
Decision: prototype range plus optional alert; measure before rollout

Performance and review cost

Scope screening and segmenting are O(N) in the transcript records; direct coding against K codes can be O(NK). Participant deduplication across M coded excerpts is O(M) expected time with a set. Human reviewers should inspect every disputed span and a sample of accepted labels. The project passes only when each theme has segment references, its contrary cases, a stable codebook version, reconciled counts, and an explicit boundary between interview evidence and product hypothesis.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not export incidental identifiers for an unrelated use.
  • Do not discard P-03's correction or P-11's counterexample.
  • Do not count nine excerpts as nine people.
  • Do not claim a prototype has already reduced missed pickups.

title: Forecast prompts: define target, horizon, and time grain
summary: Specify exactly what quantity is predicted and when it becomes final.
body:
A forecasting prompt needs a target with units, entity key, time grain, forecast origin, horizon, and data-finalization rule. A request for 'next week's demand' is ambiguous if the source records orders by local day but the planner buys kits by depot-week. The application should convert timestamps to the agreed depot calendar, aggregate once, and provide a typed series. The model can explain the contract or flag a missing field; it should not improvise the calendar boundary. Preserve whether the target is submitted orders, fulfilled orders, or consumed stock. Those measures answer different operating questions.

Operational case

Aster Repair plans weekly replacement-kit inventory for depot D-47. Each week runs Monday 00:00 through the next Monday 00:00 in the depot's local time zone. The target is fulfilled kits, not submitted requests. At the Sunday 18:00 planning origin, the current week has not finished, so the next complete week is the forecast target. A prompt that treats Sunday's partial count as a full week will understate demand. The contract marks unfinished periods as partial and excludes them from a full-week baseline.

Entity: depot D-47
Target: fulfilled replacement kits, count
Grain: depot-local Monday-to-Monday week
Origin: Sunday 18:00 local
Horizon: next complete week
Current week: partial, not a completed observation

Performance and review cost

Converting and aggregating N event records by entity and local week is O(N) expected time with a keyed map and O(W) storage for W resulting weeks. Calendar conversion deserves an explicit test near time-zone changes; one wrong boundary can alter several weekly totals. Keep the source event count and aggregation version beside the series so an analyst can reproduce the target before debating models.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not mix submitted orders with fulfilled kits.
  • Do not treat a partial week as a complete observation.
  • Do not leave the depot calendar implicit.
