questions.explanation: The person needs a readable repair instruction.

questions.prompt: Does visible status text prove it was announced?
options: No, verify with the intended interaction
questions.explanation: Visible and spoken feedback are different observations.

options: Measure the effective rendered color pair
Use the design token name only
questions.explanation: The rendered foreground and background govern the measurement.

When a developer says it is fixed

Report it as a confirmed failure

title: Analytics prompts: define the metric and event contract
summary: Name the unit, eligibility, event trigger, completion rule, and time window before generating a chart.
body:
A product metric is a rule over observations, not a label on a dashboard. The prompt should specify the business question, analysis unit, inclusion and exclusion rules, event names, trigger points, identity key, completion window, and denominator. Ask the model to return unresolved definitions before analysis. Instrumentation can fire on page render, button press, or a confirmed server action; those are not interchangeable. Keep the contract version with the output so a later event rename or trigger change does not silently rewrite the historical series.

Operational case

Meridian asks whether signup is easier on mobile. 'Signup start' originally fires on page load, including refreshes, while 'signup complete' fires after server confirmation. The analyst changes the question to eligible unique users who start and then complete within the chosen window. The event contract identifies the start trigger, completion trigger, platform at start, and stable user identity. The model can expose this mismatch before anyone plots a rate.

Unit: eligible unique user
Start: confirmed entry to signup flow
Complete: server-confirmed account creation
Window: 24 hours after each start
Platform: value at first eligible start

Performance and review cost

Validating E event definitions is O(E) contract review, while a full record scan is O(N) for N events. The extra definition work prevents a fast but meaningless chart. A model may propose a contract, yet engineering must verify that actual emitters follow it on every client and that server-confirmed outcomes are recorded exactly as intended.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not divide a server completion count by page-render events without an identity rule.
  • Do not leave the completion window implicit.
  • Do not rename an event without recording a version break.

title: Analytics prompts: reconcile identities, duplicates, and late arrivals
summary: Count people only after event deliveries and identity changes have been reconciled.
body:
An event stream may retry delivery, arrive out of order, and change identity when an anonymous visitor signs in. A prompt for analysis should name the deduplication key, identity-stitching policy, late-arrival cutoff, and treatment of missing keys. The model can flag suspicious count gaps, but deterministic processing must perform the merge and record what was excluded. A unique event ID removes retry duplicates; it does not by itself establish a unique person. Keep the raw count, deduplicated event count, and eligible-user count as separate ledger lines.

Operational case

Meridian sees 5,170 raw signup-start deliveries. An event-ID pass removes 470 retry copies, leaving 4,700 start events in this synthetic dataset. The analyst then verifies that each represents one eligible user under the chosen identity policy; only then can 4,700 be called unique starts. A late completion arriving after the reporting cutoff is held for the next run or handled by a documented restatement rule, not quietly inserted into a published denominator.

Raw deliveries 5,170
Retry copies by stable event ID 470
Deduplicated starts 4,700
Identity review: 4,700 eligible unique users in this packet
Late arrivals: cutoff and restatement rule recorded

Performance and review cost

Hash-based deduplication of N events is O(N) expected time and O(N) memory. Sorting by event time is O(N log N) when ordered session reconstruction is required. Identity stitching can be much harder if keys are missing or reused, so the report must state its confidence and exclusions rather than claiming exact user counts from an arbitrary event total.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate unique events with unique people without checking identity.
  • Do not silently mix late events into a locked report.
  • Do not discard every event with a missing key without recording the exclusion.

title: Analytics prompts: enforce funnel eligibility and event order
summary: Count completions only for users who entered the defined step and met its window.
body:
A funnel rate requires a declared start population, ordered steps, completion deadline, and rules for repeated attempts. The numerator must be a subset of the denominator. Ask the model to inspect whether a table satisfies those invariants, then compute the rate outside free text. A completion event before the chosen start, or a completion from an excluded account, cannot be included merely because its name matches. Choose whether the unit is user, session, or attempt and keep it constant through every step.

Operational case

For Meridian's 4,700 eligible unique starts, 2,820 users complete within 24 hours. The rate is 2,820/4,700, or 60%. A second signup attempt by the same person stays under the documented user-level rule rather than creating another person. A completion recorded after 24 hours is excluded from this rate but may appear in a separately named longer-window measure. The model's summary must carry the window and unit beside 60%.

Denominator: 4,700 eligible unique starting users
Numerator: 2,820 of those users complete within 24 hours
Rate: 2,820 / 4,700 = 60%
Invariant: completion users are a subset of starting users
Repeat attempt: handled by user-level rule

Performance and review cost

A hash join of start and completion records by user ID is O(N) expected time and O(U) memory for N events and U users. An ordered multi-step funnel may need O(N log N) sorting. The prompt's word count is negligible compared with the cost of getting event order and eligibility wrong; test those invariants before generating a polished chart.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not count completions from users outside the start set.
  • Do not switch from users to attempts mid-funnel.
  • Do not omit the 24-hour completion window.

title: Analytics prompts: pin cohort windows and time zones
summary: Keep membership, exposure, and observation periods stable across comparisons.
body:
A cohort is defined by a membership event and a time boundary. Prompting for a retention or conversion comparison must identify that event, the time zone used for bucketing, the observation horizon, data cutoff, and how incomplete cohorts are marked. A calendar-day label and a rolling 24-hour window answer different questions. Never compare a mature cohort with a recent cohort whose users have not had equal time to complete. The model can draft a cohort table schema, but the timestamp conversion and eligibility calculation belong in tested code.

Operational case

Meridian's report closes at midnight in the reporting time zone. A signup started at 23:50 may complete shortly after midnight while still falling within its personal 24-hour window. If the analyst buckets starts by local day but cuts completions at the same midnight, the final cohort is incomplete. The release table marks that cohort provisional until all users have had the full 24 hours plus the documented late-arrival allowance.

Membership: first eligible signup start
Bucket: reporting-zone calendar date
Outcome: complete within personal 24-hour window
Cutoff: end of outcome window plus late-arrival allowance
Recent cohort: provisional, not compared as mature

Performance and review cost

Bucketing N events after timestamp normalization is O(N); joining each user's outcome is O(N) expected time with an indexed identity map. Waiting for a mature window delays publication but avoids a false decline. Store UTC instants and the reporting-zone rule so a daylight-saving transition or boundary event can be replayed consistently.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not compare an immature cohort with a fully observed cohort.
  • Do not confuse local calendar days with rolling 24-hour windows.
  • Do not erase the reporting time zone from the chart caption.

title: Analytics prompts: review read-only queries and totals
summary: Constrain generated queries, test joins, and reconcile outputs before explanation.
body:
A query-writing prompt should state the schema, allowed read-only tables, row-level privacy constraints, metric contract, and expected checks. Treat generated SQL as a proposal. Review joins for accidental multiplication, verify unique keys, limit scanned dates, and compare grouped totals with a separately computed control. Do not execute an unrestricted query against production simply because the model supplied it. The final explanation should consume a locked result table, not improvise arithmetic or silently change filters between versions.

Operational case

Meridian's platform query reports 2,350 eligible mobile starts and 2,350 desktop starts. Their sum matches 4,700. It reports 1,175 and 1,645 completions, summing to 2,820. A careless join against a device-history table could duplicate users who changed devices; the analyst first assigns platform at each user's first eligible start, then checks one row per user before grouping. The query remains read-only and uses a bounded reporting interval.

Mobile starts 2,350 + desktop starts 2,350 = 4,700
Mobile completes 1,175 + desktop completes 1,645 = 2,820
Key check: one row per eligible user before grouping
Query scope: read-only, bounded date interval
Release: totals reconciled to control

Performance and review cost

A bounded scan is O(N) in relevant rows; hash aggregation is O(N) expected time and O(G) memory for G groups. A bad many-to-many join can inflate intermediate rows far beyond N, making both cost and conclusions wrong. Validate cardinality and scan scope before asking the model to interpret the output.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not run generated SQL without reviewing joins and permissions.
  • Do not accept segment sums that fail to match the control total.
  • Do not group raw retry deliveries as unique users.

title: Analytics prompts: explain segment gaps without inventing causes
summary: Separate a measured difference from a mechanism or intervention claim.
body:
A segment comparison needs the same eligibility, identity, event definition, and observation window on both sides. Ask the model to report counts and rates, identify possible measurement or composition differences, and propose targeted checks. A descriptive gap is not proof of a design defect or of the effect of a planned fix. Seasonality, device mix, acquisition channels, missing events, and changed instrumentation are plausible alternatives. The memo should rank next tests by information value and leave the causal field unresolved until stronger evidence exists.

Operational case

Meridian's mobile signup rate is 1,175/2,350, or 50%; desktop is 1,645/2,350, or 70%. The gap is 20 percentage points. The analyst can investigate mobile form errors, client event loss, traffic sources, and version exposure, but the numbers alone do not show which mechanism is responsible. A product proposal to shorten the mobile form is a testable hypothesis, not a result already supported by this table.

Mobile: 1,175 / 2,350 = 50%
Desktop: 1,645 / 2,350 = 70%
Difference: 20 percentage points
Observed: segment gap
Unknown: cause and effect of a proposed form change

Performance and review cost

Comparing two grouped rates is O(1) arithmetic after an O(N) data preparation pass. Investigating confounders costs additional slices, logging checks, and often a controlled study. Keep a compact hypothesis ledger so the model does not repeat a single attractive explanation as fact across successive reports.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call the 20-point gap a proven mobile form defect.
  • Do not hide the two 2,350-person denominators.
  • Do not compare segments built with different identity rules.

title: Analytics prompts: turn a metric packet into a bounded decision
summary: Ship a decision memo with traceable figures, uncertainties, owner, and follow-up measure.
body:
An analytics memo should carry the metric contract version, source snapshot, denominator ledger, segment table, data-quality checks, uncertainty, decision owner, and proposed next observation. Prompt the model to draft claims only from locked figures and to name what cannot yet be inferred. A release gate should fail if a segment total does not reconcile, an immature cohort is presented as final, or a hypothesis becomes a causal claim. If a product change proceeds, define its success measure before exposure and monitor instrumentation health alongside outcome metrics.

Operational case

Meridian's memo states that 2,820 of 4,700 eligible starting users completed within 24 hours. It reports 50% mobile and 70% desktop, with a 20-point gap. The decision is to inspect mobile errors and event delivery, then design a controlled test for a shorter form if the measurement holds. The memo does not say the new form will improve conversion. An owner records the query snapshot and schedules a recheck after the last cohort matures.

Claim: 2,820 / 4,700 = 60% within 24 hours
Segments: mobile 50%; desktop 70%; gap 20 points
Decision: inspect errors and event delivery
Hypothesis: shorter form may help; unproven
Gate: totals, cohort maturity, and owner verified

Performance and review cost

Reconciling C claims with an indexed result ledger is O(C) lookups plus review time; monitoring N new events is O(N) processing. A concise decision memo reduces repeated analytical work when it stores the contract and query version. Do not optimize for a persuasive narrative at the expense of reproducibility or a clear unknown state.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not publish a causal headline from an observational funnel.
  • Do not omit a query or metric version from the handoff.
  • Do not set a success target after viewing the intervention result.

title: Project: reconcile Meridian's signup funnel
summary: Apply the full product analytics evidence contract to a fictional product packet.
body:
A product-analytics prompt should preserve metric definitions, event lineage, eligibility, identity, and time windows. It can explain a validated table and suggest checks. It cannot turn raw event volume into a user count or infer causation from a descriptive funnel. Meridian Parcel is a fictional product used throughout these lessons.

Review the packet

Meridian records 5,170 raw signup-start events. After removing 470 duplicate deliveries by event ID, 4,700 eligible unique users remain for the chosen window. Of those users, 2,820 complete signup within the defined period, giving a 60% funnel rate. The mobile group has 2,350 starts and 1,175 completions, or 50%; desktop also has 2,350 starts but 1,645 completions, or 70%. The prompt must preserve these denominators and show a product hypothesis as a hypothesis, not a causal verdict.

Raw start events: 5,170; duplicate event deliveries: 470
Eligible unique starts: 4,700
Mobile: 1,175 / 2,350 = 50%
Desktop: 1,645 / 2,350 = 70%
All: 2,820 / 4,700 = 60%
Cause of gap: unknown without further evidence

Performance and review cost

Deduplicating N events by stable event ID is O(N) expected time and O(N) memory; grouping U eligible users by platform is O(U) with a small number of counters. The expensive part is proving that the event contract and identity rules mean what the labels claim. Preserve a reproducible query and its input snapshot so the memo can be rerun after an instrumentation repair.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use 5,170 raw event deliveries as the eligible-user denominator.
  • Do not average the two platform percentages when segment sizes differ.
  • Do not call a platform gap a proven design cause.

title: Localization prompts: define the locale and message contract
summary: Pin target locale, catalog version, message purpose, and review state before translating.
body:
A localization prompt should state the target language and region, catalog version, message key, product state, audience, terminology owner, and output format. A locale label is not a license to guess business meaning: the same word can name a delivery slot, a storage window, or a browser window. Provide enough UI context and keep the source string beside its key. Ask the model to mark ambiguous terms for a language reviewer instead of choosing a fluent but unsupported interpretation. The final artifact is a versioned candidate, not a verified translation.

Operational case

Harbor has 47 delivery-notice keys in catalog H-47. HP-07 concerns the time range a recipient may choose before confirming delivery, not the period a parcel stays at a collection point. The request supplies the screen, control purpose, locale, and variable schema. The model flags 'window' as ambiguous until the product owner confirms the intended action. That short clarification protects every later translation and avoids a misleading notice on the confirmation screen.

Catalog H-47 | key HP-07 | state: before delivery confirmation
Audience: recipient | target locale: ar-EG
Meaning of window: selectable delivery time range
Variables: {deliveryWindow} | unresolved terms: stop for review

Performance and review cost

Inspecting N keys against a context ledger is O(N) review work; a shared glossary reduces repeated interpretation but still needs version control. Adding context fields costs a small amount of prompt space and prevents expensive retranslation. Keep sensitive recipient data out of examples, and use synthetic parcel details when demonstrating the rendered message.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not translate an ambiguous product term without its screen context.
  • Do not mix catalog versions in one approval packet.
  • Do not treat a model candidate as language review.

title: Localization prompts: preserve variables and plural branches
summary: Compare message structure before judging the phrasing of a localized string.
body:
A message can sound natural yet fail at runtime because a required variable disappeared or a plural branch is missing. Give the model the message schema, variable types, and supported categories, then require a structural diff before language review. Placeholder names are application contracts; they are not free words to translate. Plural selection belongs to the locale-aware message engine, not an English singular-versus-other shortcut invented in prose. Test representative boundary counts in the actual engine and keep the rendered result in the review packet.

Operational case

Harbor's HP-07 candidate omits {deliveryWindow}, so the notice cannot show the selected time. HP-12 has a count-dependent message but lacks a category the selected locale requires. The reviewer first catches the missing variable and branch by comparing parsed message structures, then renders several count values to inspect grammar and layout. A model may propose repairs, but the catalog parser and language reviewer must accept them before the key moves to pass.

HP-07 required: {deliveryWindow}; candidate: missing
HP-12 required: locale-specific plural branches; candidate: incomplete
Gate 1: parse and compare message structure
Gate 2: render boundary counts and review language

Performance and review cost

Parsing N message patterns is O(total pattern length); set comparison of V placeholders is O(V) expected time per key. Rendering several count cases per plural message adds a small, deliberate test matrix. This is cheaper than discovering a blank runtime value after publication, and it keeps linguistic judgment separate from deterministic structure checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not translate placeholder identifiers.
  • Do not infer every locale's plural behavior from English.
  • Do not approve a structurally valid message without rendered language review.

title: Localization prompts: test mixed-direction identifiers
summary: Keep parcel IDs, names, and punctuation readable inside right-to-left notices.
body:
A right-to-left interface can contain left-to-right identifiers and user-entered names. The prompt should preserve the identifier bytes, state the base direction, and ask for the rendered ordering to be checked in context. String reversal is not localization. Markup or component behavior must isolate a mixed-direction token where needed; punctuation around it may otherwise appear in a confusing position. A text-only model can suggest test cases, but the browser render and assistive interaction determine whether the actual notice remains intelligible.

Operational case

HP-18 places parcel code PK-47A next to right-to-left notice text. In the first build, punctuation appears detached from the code in one message state. Harbor keeps the code unchanged and repairs the component's direction handling around the inserted value. The reviewer checks the short code, a longer code, and a recipient name with mixed-script characters. The fix is accepted only after those values render correctly in the actual notice surface.

HP-18 | base direction: right-to-left
Inserted token: PK-47A, exact bytes retained
Observed: adjacent punctuation rendered ambiguously
Repair target: isolate inserted token in the component
Retest: short, long, and mixed-script values

Performance and review cost

Testing K inserted-token shapes over S message states costs O(KS) render checks. Most code changes are in one shared component, but each distinct insertion context still needs a check. A screenshot can document visual order; keyboard selection and spoken behavior may require separate inspection when they affect the user task.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not reverse the identifier characters.
  • Do not assume a translated string fixes component direction handling.
  • Do not test only one short Latin code.

title: Localization prompts: render typed dates, numbers, and units
summary: Keep the underlying value separate from its locale-specific display text.
body:
A model should not retype a timestamp, quantity, or currency amount into a locale-looking string and then use that string as data. Give it a typed value, its unit or time zone, the target locale, and the intended display role. The application formatter performs rendering; the prompt reviews the result and flags ambiguous labels. A date-only delivery promise differs from an instant in time, and a currency symbol without a code may be unclear across regions. Preserve the machine value and the rendered value together for audit.

Operational case

HP-29 shows a delivery instant with a numeric date that could be read in two orders. Harbor retains the underlying timestamp and reporting time zone, then asks the formatter to render a target-locale label. The review compares that label with the schedule confirmation and checks whether the day boundary changed correctly. It does not ask a model to guess an instant from an ambiguous source string. A count of 47 parcels likewise stays numeric until the display layer formats it.

HP-29 input: typed delivery instant + explicit time zone
Display: target-locale date and time from formatter
Audit: retain instant and rendered label together
Reject: ambiguous numeric date parsed by guesswork

Performance and review cost

Formatting N independent values is O(N) application work; testing boundary instants adds a small fixed set per time zone. Keeping typed source fields costs storage but prevents repeated parse errors. The review prompt should spend its tokens on display ambiguities and missing context, not on manual recalculation the runtime can perform consistently.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not parse an ambiguous date without an explicit source format.
  • Do not use localized display text as a stored numeric value.
  • Do not drop the time zone from an instant-based promise.

title: Localization prompts: reconcile terminology and tone
summary: Keep product terms consistent while allowing a language reviewer to resolve meaning.
body:
A glossary is a decision record, not a command to replace every occurrence of a word mechanically. Give each term its concept, product context, approved rendering, prohibited alternatives, and version. Ask the model to flag inconsistencies and awkward register, then route disputed cases to a native language reviewer with the screen and action attached. A support notice, error, and marketing line may require different tone even when they share terminology. The reviewer should approve the meaning and user action, not merely grammatical smoothness.

Operational case

Harbor uses one approved term for a delivery time range in confirmation notices. A candidate for a failed-delivery message uses a word that instead suggests storage duration. The model flags the glossary conflict; the language reviewer checks the screen and adjusts the message so the recipient understands the next action. The product owner updates the glossary decision for future keys. HP-07 remains blocked until its placeholder and meaning both pass.

Concept: selectable delivery time range
Catalog: H-47 | affected: HP-07 and related notices
Model output: terminology conflict flagged
Human decision: approved wording with screen context
Glossary version: recorded before release

Performance and review cost

Comparing N strings to a glossary of indexed terms is O(N) passes plus the cost of disputed-case review. False positives occur when one surface uses a term in a different sense, so a human decides those cases. The glossary reduces future rework only if each approved change is versioned and propagated to all affected strings.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not enforce a glossary term without its concept and context.
  • Do not treat fluent grammar as proof of correct product meaning.
  • Do not close a dispute without recording the reviewer decision.

title: Localization prompts: use pseudolocale and real layout checks
summary: Find hard-coded text and clipped controls before and after translation review.
body:
Pseudolocalization can expose text baked into a component, length assumptions, and untranslated fragments before language review. A prompt can specify test states and turn screenshots into candidate findings, but the rendered interface decides whether controls remain readable and operable. Test long labels, narrow widths, zoom, form errors, and dialogs. Do not confuse a pseudolocale pass with a real locale pass: the latter still needs script, direction, plural, input-method, and language checks. Record the viewport and state for every clipping report.

Operational case

Harbor's HP-41 notice fits in the default desktop card but clips its final action at a narrow viewport after translation. A pseudolocale had already warned that the button width was fixed. The reviewer captures the real localized build at the failing width and traces the hidden action through keyboard focus. The component owner changes wrapping and sizing; the reviewer repeats the state with a long recipient name rather than approving a static screenshot alone.

HP-41 | state: delivery notice with final action
Viewport: narrow; zoom and long name included
Observed: action clipped by fixed-width card
Repair: component wraps without hiding the action
Retest: real locale plus keyboard operation

Performance and review cost

A matrix of V viewport settings, S states, and L locales requires O(VSL) targeted render checks. Shared component tests reduce repetition but do not replace a real translated page review. Prioritize states with required actions and known long strings; a huge screenshot set without interaction evidence can still miss a blocked task.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a pseudolocale pass a language approval.
  • Do not inspect only desktop idle state.
  • Do not accept an action that is visible but cannot be operated.

title: Localization prompts: gate release on catalog and rendered retests
summary: Reconcile key coverage, owners, and fixed states before approving a locale.
body:
A localization release packet needs the source and target catalog versions, changed-key list, placeholder and plural checks, language-review status, rendered-state evidence, open defects, and named approval. The prompt may summarize that packet, but it must not convert missing checks into a pass. Count distinct failed keys, not screenshots or repeated observations, and preserve each finding's owner and retest path. A fix to a shared renderer can close several failures only after every affected state is checked against the same release build.

Operational case

Harbor's H-47 packet has 47 keys. Forty-two pass, while HP-07, HP-12, HP-18, HP-29, and HP-41 each fail a different gate. A reviewer assigns the first two to message owners, mixed direction and clipping to component owners, and date ambiguity to the formatter owner. After repairs, the packet records the new catalog and build versions plus retest evidence for all five. Until then, the localized release remains blocked regardless of a polished summary.

H-47: 47 keys = 42 pass + 5 failed distinct keys
Open: HP-07, HP-12, HP-18, HP-29, HP-41
Required: owner, fixed build, rendered retest, language review
Decision now: do not release the locale

Performance and review cost

Set comparison between source and target catalogs is O(N) expected time for N keys; retesting F failed keys adds at least O(F) targeted checks. A release ledger saves time by narrowing inspection to changed and affected states, but shared-component changes still warrant broader regression samples. No prompt wording can replace missing runtime or language evidence.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not count five screenshots of one defect as five distinct failed keys.
  • Do not approve a locale with an untested required action.
  • Do not omit the catalog and build versions from a retest receipt.

title: Project: review Harbor's localized delivery notices
summary: Apply the full localization qa evidence contract to a fictional release packet.
body:
Review a fictional Harbor Parcel release packet containing 47 notice strings for a second locale. The prompt organizes checks, but the translation engine, browser, and language reviewer decide whether the actual product behaves correctly. Five distinct keys fail for different reasons; the other 42 pass this packet's checks. A clean English preview does not establish that the localized release is ready.

Review the packet

Key HP-07 drops a required delivery-window placeholder; HP-12 lacks a needed plural form for the selected locale; HP-18 places a Latin parcel identifier in right-to-left text without reliable isolation; HP-29 renders a delivery instant with an ambiguous date label; and HP-41 is clipped at narrow width. The reviewer locks the catalog version, locale, route, and test data, assigns each failure to a component or message owner, and retests all five. The release stays blocked until the actual rendered paths and language review pass. None of the five failures is repaired merely by rewriting a summary.

Catalog H-47: 47 keys; 42 pass; 5 distinct failed keys
HP-07 placeholder | HP-12 plural | HP-18 mixed direction
HP-29 date rendering | HP-41 narrow-width clipping
Release: blocked pending owner repair and rendered retest

Performance and review cost

A first pass over N message keys is O(N); rendering L locales across S important states adds O(LS) review cases, with more cases for plural and viewport boundaries. Human language review remains a separate cost because syntactic parity does not establish meaning. Preserve the five key IDs and exact render states so the follow-up check is targeted rather than an unbounded reread of every string.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call 42 passing keys a releasable packet while five required keys fail.
  • Do not replace actual locale rendering with a model's translation confidence.
  • Do not close a finding until the affected route and state are retested.

title: Experiment prompts: fix hypothesis, unit, and exposure
summary: State what changes, who is randomized, and when an assignment becomes exposure.
body:
An experiment prompt should name the product hypothesis, control behavior, treatment behavior, assignment unit, eligibility rule, exposure event, outcome window, and intended decision. Randomizing a user while measuring sessions can produce repeated correlated rows if the analysis forgets the user key. Assignment is not exposure: a person can be assigned but never load the changed surface, or the exposure log can fail. Keep these populations separate and decide the primary analysis rule before examining results. The model can expose missing definitions, but it cannot repair inconsistent assignment IDs by persuasive wording.

Operational case

Aster tests a shorter signup form. The randomization unit is an eligible user at signup entry; the treatment is the shortened form, while control retains the current form. There are 4,800 assigned users per arm. Exposure logs contain only 4,600 control and 4,500 treatment records. The analyst does not switch to logged exposure as the denominator merely to make the treatment look stronger. They investigate logging before accepting an effect claim.

Hypothesis: shorter form may change 24h signup completion
Unit: eligible assigned user at signup entry
Assigned: 4,800 control; 4,800 treatment
Exposure logs: 4,600 and 4,500; reason unknown
Primary unit and window: frozen before analysis

Performance and review cost

Mapping N assignments to exposure and outcome rows is O(N) expected time and O(N) memory. Defining the unit early prevents a more expensive reinterpretation after the result is known. A model can draft a contract checklist, but instrumentation and assignment-service logs must be inspected independently when their populations disagree.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use sessions as independent users without a declared rule.
  • Do not equate assignment with confirmed exposure.
  • Do not choose the denominator after seeing the outcome.

title: Experiment prompts: investigate assignment and exposure imbalance
summary: Check configured split, assigned counts, and logged exposure before reading outcomes.
body:
The prompt should request the configured allocation, unique assigned-unit counts, identity exclusions, and exposure-log counts for each arm. An apparent sample-ratio mismatch is a data-quality symptom; it is not automatically a product effect or a verdict about randomization. Use a prespecified statistical check where the experiment platform supports one, but first inspect duplicate IDs, bot filters, missing events, and variant-specific logging. Do not declare a formal mismatch from two numbers without the allocation rule and check result. Keep the investigation outcome attached to the analysis packet.

Operational case

Aster intended a 1:1 assignment and observes exactly 4,800 unique assigned users in each arm. That count alone does not validate exposure logging: the recorded exposures are 4,600 and 4,500. The model lists plausible failure paths, such as variant-specific event loss or different eligibility at the surface. An engineer checks the emitters and the analyst verifies identity filters. Until the discrepancy is explained, the effect memo remains provisional.

Configured assignment 1:1
Observed assigned 4,800 : 4,800
Logged exposure 4,600 : 4,500
Status: investigate missing or unequal exposure records
Do not label a formal SRM without the planned check

Performance and review cost

Counting N unique assignments and exposures with hashed IDs is O(N) expected time and O(N) memory. Additional joins across client and server logs can dominate the investigation cost. Automated alerts are useful triage, but a reviewer must establish whether the mismatch comes from assignment, filtering, or telemetry before interpreting the outcome table.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not read the outcome delta before resolving a serious data-quality flag.
  • Do not treat equal assigned counts as proof every user saw the intended surface.
  • Do not call an unequal log count a formal statistical mismatch without its test.

title: Experiment prompts: freeze the primary metric and guardrails
summary: Declare one decision metric, harm checks, and observation window before launch.
body:
An experiment plan should define a primary metric, its unit and denominator, guardrails for likely harms, minimum run or observation window, analysis method, and decision threshold before assignment begins. The model can draft the plan and identify missing fields, but a human owner approves it. An unplanned metric discovered after looking at many outcomes is exploratory, not the same evidence as a preregistered primary measure. Guardrails are part of the release decision even when the primary metric moves in the hoped-for direction.

Operational case

Aster's primary outcome is signup completion within 24 hours per assigned eligible user. Its support-ticket rate is a guardrail because a shorter form may omit needed guidance. The packet later shows 48% versus 52% completion and 2% versus 3% support tickets. Those numbers are descriptive until the approved analysis and data-quality checks run. Aster cannot rewrite the plan to ignore support tickets after seeing the increase.

Primary: 24h completion / assigned eligible users
Guardrail: support tickets / assigned eligible users
Analysis and decision threshold: locked before launch
Exploratory slices: labeled separately
Plan changes: versioned, not silently backdated

Performance and review cost

Checking M planned metrics across N assigned users is O(MN) in a naive scan or O(N+M) with a prepared per-user fact table and indexed aggregates. Planning is cheap compared with arguing over a favorable post hoc metric. Keep the frozen plan and every later amendment visible in the review packet.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not select a primary metric after seeing all outcomes.
  • Do not omit a plausible harm measure from the decision.
  • Do not confuse an exploratory slice with a planned confirmatory test.

title: Experiment prompts: reconcile missing outcomes by assigned unit
summary: Keep assigned users visible when exposure or outcome logging is incomplete.
body:
Missing events can arise from product behavior, delayed ingestion, client loss, or a broken emitter. A prompt for experiment analysis should request a disposition table by assigned arm: assigned IDs, exposure records, outcome records, late arrivals, exclusions, and reasons. A missing outcome is not always a failure to complete; that interpretation requires a trusted server-side outcome path and an observation window that has matured. Avoid a complete-case comparison that silently drops users with missing telemetry, because missingness may differ by variant.

Operational case

Aster sees 4,800 assigned users in each arm but fewer exposure logs. The team verifies whether 24-hour completion comes from a server-confirmed account record rather than the same incomplete client channel. It lists missing exposure IDs by variant and checks whether those users have outcomes. If the missingness is variant-specific, the analyst cannot simply use 4,600 and 4,500 as clean observed populations. The memo holds the uncertainty until the data path is understood.

Arm ledger: assigned | exposure logged | outcome observed
Control: 4,800 | 4,600 | verify server outcome path
Treatment: 4,800 | 4,500 | verify server outcome path
Late records and exclusions: count with reasons
Analysis status: provisional while missingness unresolved

Performance and review cost

Joining N assignment IDs with outcome and exposure tables is O(N) expected time with indexed keys and O(N) memory for the reconciliation ledger. Missingness review can require engineering traces rather than another aggregate query. Preserve the assigned population in the packet even if some events cannot yet be classified.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat every absent client event as a real noncompletion.
  • Do not compare only complete telemetry rows without checking variant bias.
  • Do not hide late-arrival and exclusion counts.

title: Experiment prompts: separate effect size from uncertainty
summary: Report the observed difference, then apply the planned inference method outside prose.
body:
A treatment-control difference is a descriptive estimate. An experiment claim also needs the planned uncertainty method, randomization and data-quality checks, observation cutoff, and handling of repeated looks or many tested outcomes. Have code calculate the effect and its uncertainty from a locked dataset; the model should explain the result without fabricating a confidence interval or p-value. If the team repeatedly checks results and stops at the first favorable number, an ordinary one-time test no longer has its advertised error behavior. Preserve the planned stopping rule and all reviewed looks.

Operational case

Aster's assigned-user rates are 2,304/4,800 = 48% for control and 2,496/4,800 = 52% for treatment. The observed difference is four percentage points. The packet does not include a checked interval or a completed exposure-log investigation, so the model may report the descriptive numbers but cannot claim a verified lift. Aster also records when interim reviews occurred; it does not present the most favorable day as the final planned readout.

Control 2,304 / 4,800 = 48%
Treatment 2,496 / 4,800 = 52%
Observed difference = +4 percentage points
Checked interval or test result: absent
Inference claim: withheld

Performance and review cost

Computing two rates from validated counters is O(1); preparing the per-user table is O(N) for N assigned users. Uncertainty calculations depend on the prespecified design and may be more complex when units are clustered or outcomes are correlated. The prompt should keep the arithmetic and inference artifacts separate so a reviewer can reproduce each one.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not invent a confidence interval from an aggregate summary.
  • Do not equate four percentage points with statistical certainty.
  • Do not hide repeated interim looks.

title: Experiment prompts: investigate slices and guardrail movement
summary: Treat subgroup stories as exploratory unless the comparison was planned and checked.
body:
Segmenting an experiment after a surprising result can help diagnose a mechanism, but every extra slice offers another chance to see noise. A prompt should distinguish prespecified subgroups from exploratory investigations, keep denominators and assignment rules on both sides, and record whether the slice was chosen before or after outcome review. A guardrail movement deserves its own validity and practical-impact check. Do not dismiss a possible harm solely because the primary metric improved; the joint release decision must consider both.

Operational case

Aster has 96 support tickets among 4,800 control users, or 2%, and 144 among 4,800 treatment users, or 3%. The observed guardrail difference is one percentage point. The analyst checks ticket taxonomy, duplicate reports, attribution window, and whether form confusion could explain the movement. A model may suggest a mobile slice, but unless it was planned, that slice is exploratory and cannot rescue a blocked rollout by itself.

Support guardrail: control 96/4,800 = 2%
Treatment 144/4,800 = 3%
Observed difference: +1 percentage point
Investigate taxonomy, duplicates, window, and mechanism
Post hoc slices: exploratory labels retained

Performance and review cost

Scanning N ticket records and assignment IDs is O(N) expected time with indexed joins; K subgroup analyses can multiply compute and review costs. The more important cost is interpretive: many unplanned slices make one attractive story easy to find. Keep a slice ledger and require a separate confirmation plan for a new subgroup hypothesis.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not ignore the higher ticket rate because completion increased.
  • Do not promote a post hoc subgroup story to the primary result.
  • Do not compare ticket counts without the assigned-user denominators.

title: Experiment prompts: gate rollout on a reproducible packet
summary: Make the ship, hold, or revert decision traceable to the frozen plan and verified logs.
body:
A final experiment memo should include the plan version, assignment and exposure counts, outcome definitions, data-quality investigations, effect and uncertainty artifacts, guardrails, open issues, decision owner, and follow-up monitoring. Prompt the model to draft only from that locked packet. A persuasive headline cannot substitute for a verified exposure path or a guardrail review. If a staged rollout is approved later, record its audience, duration, stop conditions, and monitoring ownership before changing traffic. The current decision may be hold even when the observed primary difference is favorable.

Operational case

Aster's packet shows a four-point descriptive completion advantage for treatment, but its exposure records are incomplete and treatment support tickets are one point higher. The approved memo does not call the shorter form successful. The owner holds rollout, checks exposure emitters and ticket classification, recomputes the planned analysis, and reviews uncertainty before any traffic change. A later approval would need a separate staged rollout record and monitoring receipt.

Primary descriptive difference: +4 percentage points
Exposure discrepancy: unresolved
Support guardrail: +1 percentage point in treatment
Decision: hold; verify logs and harm signal
Future rollout: only after new reviewed packet

Performance and review cost

Reconciling C memo claims against indexed tables is O(C) lookups plus review time; staged monitoring processes N new events in O(N). The packet prevents repeated debate over which numbers were used. Do not let the model fill missing uncertainty or approval fields with plausible text merely to complete a template.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not ship from a favorable descriptive rate alone.
  • Do not erase the unresolved exposure discrepancy.
  • Do not imply a staged rollout occurred without its receipt.

title: Project: review Aster's signup experiment
summary: Apply the full product experiments evidence contract to a fictional release packet.
body:
Review a fictional Aster Console signup experiment with two assigned groups of 4,800 users each. The prompt may draft analysis from a locked packet, but it must preserve the randomization unit, outcome window, logging checks, and planned decision rule. A descriptive difference is not a license to ship while exposure records and a support-ticket guardrail remain unresolved.

Review the packet

Control has 2,304 signup completions within 24 hours, or 48% of 4,800 assigned users. Treatment has 2,496, or 52%; the observed difference is 4 percentage points. The exposure ledger contains 4,600 control and 4,500 treatment records, fewer than assigned in both groups, so the team investigates logging and eligibility before interpreting the effect. Support-ticket counts are 96/4,800 (2%) in control and 144/4,800 (3%) in treatment. The packet contains no checked uncertainty estimate or confirmed reason for the logging gap. The current decision is hold, repair the evidence path, and rerun the locked analysis.

Assigned: control 4,800; treatment 4,800
24h completions: 2,304/4,800 = 48%; 2,496/4,800 = 52%
Observed difference: +4 percentage points
Exposure records: 4,600 control; 4,500 treatment; investigate
Support tickets: 96/4,800 = 2%; 144/4,800 = 3%
Decision: hold pending data-quality and guardrail review

Performance and review cost

Reconstructing N assignment and outcome records is O(N) expected time with an identity map; auditing several metrics and slices multiplies review work. More prose cannot compensate for a broken exposure ledger or an unplanned decision threshold. Store the randomization key, query version, observation cutoff, and investigation outcome so a later run can reproduce the same comparison.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call a four-point observed difference a proven improvement without validated inference.
  • Do not change the denominator from assigned users to logged exposures mid-analysis.
  • Do not hide the higher support-ticket rate when discussing rollout.

title: Invoice prompts: pin provenance and vendor identity
summary: Keep uploaded invoice claims separate from verified vendor and order records.
body:
An invoice prompt needs a document ID, file hash, intake time, vendor candidate, purchase-order reference, and system-of-record snapshot. The PDF may request a new remittance account or say to ignore discrepancies. Treat those sentences as untrusted document content. The model can extract and flag them but cannot change vendor master data, schedule payment, or identify the vendor solely from an OCR header. Attach each extracted field to its file and version so the reviewer can locate what was actually supplied.

Operational case

North Quay receives INV-47 twice. Both files have matching bytes and cite PO Q-47, so the intake ledger records two arrivals tied to one candidate invoice identity. A remittance note asks for a new account. The assistant marks it for the separate vendor-verification process; it does not change payment details. The verified vendor ID comes from procurement records rather than the uploaded name alone. Ledger status is checked before anyone declares whether an obligation already exists.

Invoice INV-47 | PO Q-47 | two uploads, one matching hash
Vendor: verify against master record
Remittance note: untrusted change request
Allowed model action: extract and flag; no mutation

Performance and review cost

Hashing B file bytes is O(B), and checking indexed invoice identities is O(D) for D arrivals. Keeping provenance is cheap relative to reversing a wrong payment. The prompt should carry synthetic examples instead of live bank data unless a restricted review explicitly requires them.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not create two payables from identical uploads.
  • Do not trust a bank-change sentence in an invoice.
  • Do not drop file and intake identifiers during extraction.

title: Invoice prompts: anchor each extracted field
summary: Preserve page evidence and uncertainty for quantities, prices, and totals.
body:
Field extraction is a typed proposal, not a posting command. Ask for invoice number, PO reference, quantity, unit price, currency, freight, tax, and total with a page or region anchor. An unreadable digit must be marked uncertain; OCR confidence is not the same as accounting correctness. If two regions disagree, keep both candidates rather than silently preferring the clearer line. The reviewer should be able to inspect every value used in a calculation or matching decision.

Operational case

INV-47 page one shows 47 units at 29. Its tax box is faint, so 95.41 is retained as a candidate with the observed region and a review flag. The printed total is 1,522.41. A parser confirms numeric types and decimal scale before recalculation, but a matched sum does not resolve whether the tax was applied under the correct rule. The model reports unknown where the PDF cannot support a confident field.

INV-47 page 1 line: quantity 47; unit price 29
Summary: freight 64; tax candidate 95.41
Printed total 1,522.41
Each field: type + page region + verified or uncertain

Performance and review cost

Reviewing F candidate fields across P pages is O(P+F) handling after rendering, with human time for uncertain regions. Anchors make a correction local to the disputed value. Without them, an auditor must reread the entire file and cannot distinguish an observed number from a guessed one.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not post a guessed OCR digit as verified money.
  • Do not omit field-level page anchors.
  • Do not flatten conflicting values into one confident answer.

title: Invoice prompts: recalculate typed charges
summary: Separate line amount, freight, tax, and approval state.
body:
An invoice total is computed from typed quantities, prices, discounts, freight, tax, credits, and currency under a declared rounding rule. Let decimal-safe code perform the calculation and ask the model to explain the locked result. Matching the printed total establishes arithmetic only. It does not show that freight was agreed, tax was calculated under the right rule, or goods were accepted. Keep charge types and the exact difference visible instead of returning one unlabeled amount.

Operational case

North Quay's line amount is 47 times 29, or 1,363. The stated freight 64 and stated tax 95.41 sum to a 1,522.41 invoice total, matching the printed figure. That arithmetic is correct. The packet still lacks a verified tax-basis decision and has a receiving gap. The assistant reports those gates separately; it cannot call the invoice approved just because the calculator returned zero difference.

Line: 47 × 29 = 1,363
1,363 + 64 + 95.41 = 1,522.41
Printed total: 1,522.41; arithmetic difference: 0
Tax basis and receipt match: unresolved

Performance and review cost

Summing L lines is O(L) time and O(1) working memory with a running decimal total; a traceable line ledger uses O(L) storage. The calculation is cheap. Correcting a posted misclassification is expensive, so retain every charge and its rule status for review.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use binary floating point for final money comparison.
  • Do not infer tax validity from matching arithmetic.
  • Do not hide freight inside unit price without a rule.

title: Invoice prompts: match order, receipt, and bill
summary: Identify billed quantities unsupported by accepted receipts.
body:
A three-record comparison checks purchase-order terms, accepted receipts, and invoice lines under a supplied organizational tolerance. Carry stable line IDs, units, ordered and cumulative received quantities, prior billed quantity, current bill, and agreed price. A partial shipment may be legitimate; an invoice can also cover several orders. The model should describe the precise discrepancy, while procurement and receiving systems supply the authoritative records. It must not invent a tolerance because the mismatch seems small.

Operational case

PO Q-47 orders 47 units at 29. INV-47 bills the same quantity and price, but receiving has accepted 45. Two billed units, worth 58 before other charges, lack receipt support. Receiving must determine whether the units are pending, rejected, or absent from the feed. North Quay holds the invoice while that evidence is gathered. A matching PO line does not erase the missing receipt.

PO: 47 × 29 | accepted receipt: 45
Invoice: 47 × 29
Quantity exception: 2 units; line value 58
Configured tolerance: not supplied -> hold

Performance and review cost

With indexed keys, L invoice lines need O(L) expected matching lookups; constructing cumulative receipt state costs O(R) for R events. Recording the unit and prior billing avoids false exceptions on partial deliveries. The prompt should expose missing evidence rather than guess a policy threshold.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate ordered with received quantity.
  • Do not ignore earlier bills on a split order.
  • Do not invent an acceptance tolerance.

title: Invoice prompts: distinguish duplicate ingests from credits
summary: Check file identity, business identity, ledger status, and credit records separately.
body:
Duplicate detection combines vendor ID, invoice number, file hash, amount, and ledger state. The second file may be a retry, correction, or distinct obligation. A credit note has its own identity and relation to the original bill; a model cannot subtract a hypothetical credit to make totals agree. Ask for both file-level and business-level duplicate checks and for the accounting period. Resolve ambiguous identities through the controlled payables workflow before posting.

Operational case

North Quay's second INV-47 file has the same bytes as the first, so it is a duplicate arrival. The payable ledger still must be checked to learn whether INV-47 was already posted. No credit note appears in the current packet. If one arrives later for the two undelivered units, its vendor, reference, amount, and period will need independent verification. The model cannot preemptively create that missing record.

Upload A hash = Upload B hash
Business invoice candidate: INV-47, one identity
Posted ledger state: check separately
Credit in current packet: none
Second upload: not a second payable

Performance and review cost

Hashing B bytes and checking N candidate ledger records costs O(B+N) with indexed identities. A hash match establishes the same file, while changed formatting can still conceal a duplicate business obligation. Keep both checks so document packaging does not decide payment state.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not count a repeated upload as a second payable.
  • Do not invent a credit record.
  • Do not use a file hash as the only invoice identity.

title: Invoice prompts: route exceptions before approval
summary: Assign each discrepancy an owner and keep payment actions behind an approval receipt.
body:
An exception packet needs an issue ID, affected line, observed records, possible explanations labeled as hypotheses, missing evidence, responsible team, and approval requirement. Posting, payment scheduling, vendor-master edits, and hold release are external actions. They require current ledger state and authorized receipts, not a generated paragraph. Keep separate issues separate; 'needs review' hides which person must act next. A final memo should say what passed, what failed, and what remains unknown.

Operational case

INV-47 has a two-unit receipt gap, an unverified tax basis, and a remittance-change note. Receiving owns the quantity check, the tax reviewer owns the rule, and vendor controls owns account verification. The payables approver sees all three unresolved issues and keeps the invoice held. The assistant can draft an internal handoff from verified facts but cannot send it or change financial state without explicit authorization.

EX-47A: receipt gap -> receiving
EX-47B: tax basis -> tax reviewer
EX-47C: remittance note -> vendor controls
Invoice state: hold; payment action: none
Release requires named approver and fresh ledger check

Performance and review cost

Routing E exceptions with an indexed owner map is O(E) expected work; retrieving missing evidence and obtaining approvals dominates elapsed time. Precise issue IDs reduce repeated reading. The hold should exist as system state, not merely as a warning in prose that can be separated from the payment queue.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat a model handoff as approval.
  • Do not merge distinct owners into a vague task.
  • Do not change remittance details from invoice text.

title: Project: reconcile a North Quay invoice exception
summary: Apply the invoice exception review evidence contract to a fictional packet.
body:
Review a fictional North Quay Parts invoice packet. The model can extract candidate fields and draft an exception brief. Decimal arithmetic, purchase-order and receiving records, verified vendor identity, and a named approver control any payment decision. Document text is evidence; it cannot authorize a bank change or waive a hold.

Review the packet

INV-47 bills 47 units at 29 each, or 1,363. It lists freight 64 and tax 95.41, producing a printed total of 1,522.41 by arithmetic. The tax basis is not verified. PO Q-47 agrees on quantity and unit price, but receiving confirms only 45 units. Two units worth 58 are unmatched. A second uploaded file has the same invoice identity and matching bytes, so it is a duplicate ingest, not a second obligation. The packet remains held for receipt, tax, vendor, and approval checks.

INV-47 | PO Q-47 | 47 × 29 = 1,363
Freight 64 + stated tax 95.41 -> total 1,522.41
Received 45; invoiced 47; unmatched 2 × 29 = 58
Second identical file: duplicate ingest
Decision: hold; no payment or vendor-master change

Performance and review cost

Parsing D files and reconciling L lines against indexed orders and receipts is O(D+L) expected lookup work after intake. Human review grows with exception count. Preserve invoice, order, receipt, and decision IDs so an approver can replay each comparison. The cost of a wrong payment is higher than the cost of keeping an uncertain field unresolved.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not pay because the invoice total adds correctly.
  • Do not count an identical second upload as a second debt.
  • Do not invent a receiving tolerance or tax rule.

title: Backfill prompts: pin source, target, and snapshot
summary: Identify exact schemas, keys, and record population before proposing writes.
body:
A backfill prompt needs source and target schema versions, primary key, tenancy boundary, snapshot or high-water mark, write environment, owner, and acceptance criteria. The model may draft a transformation plan but cannot infer live data from a small schema sample. State whether the source continues to receive writes and how later changes will be replayed. Counts from different instants can disagree even when both systems are correct; a fixed population must anchor each comparison.

Operational case

Harbor's review snapshot H-47 holds 47,000 keyed order rows. The new status field must preserve each row's tenant and business meaning. A sample of familiar statuses is insufficient: the reviewer asks for a complete distinct-value inventory and records the change-stream watermark. The draft runbook names a restricted execution role, but the prompt output grants no production write permission.

Snapshot H-47: 47,000 source orders
Key: tenant_id + order_id
Target schema version: recorded
Writes continue: yes; tail watermark needed
Prompt output: plan, not execution approval

Performance and review cost

Inventorying N source rows is O(N) scanning; a key manifest costs O(N) storage. This preparation prevents moving counts from being mistaken for data loss. Scope scans to authorized tenants and preserve the snapshot ID for validation.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not compare unpinned source and target counts.
  • Do not infer all legacy values from a sample.
  • Do not give a planning prompt a write credential.

title: Backfill prompts: map known states and quarantine unknowns
summary: Preserve unsupported legacy states and missing keys as reviewable exceptions.
body:
A migration mapping lists source value, target value, preconditions, null handling, owner, and test case. Unknown source states should enter a reason-coded quarantine rather than a plausible default. Ask the model to identify collisions where distinct source meanings map to one target value, then have the data owner approve any intentional loss. Deterministic code applies the versioned mapping and emits a per-row outcome. Keep the original value and row key so a corrected mapping can replay only affected records.

Operational case

Of 47,000 Harbor orders, 46,940 map under the approved rules. Forty-seven have unfamiliar legacy statuses, and 13 lack required tenant IDs; the groups are disjoint, so 60 rows are quarantined. The assistant does not call the unknown status 'pending' just to make every row load. It creates an exception ledger with reason, pseudonymous key, observed value, and owner.

47,000 = mapped 46,940 + quarantined 60
UNKNOWN_STATUS: 47 | TENANT_ID_MISSING: 13
Fallback to pending: prohibited without approval
Preserve source value and row key

Performance and review cost

Applying an indexed mapping to N rows is O(N) expected time and O(K+E) memory for K mapping keys and E exceptions. Quarantine costs review time but avoids semantic loss. A model can cluster unknown values; only an owner can authorize new meaning.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not silently default unknown statuses.
  • Do not double-count overlapping exception IDs.
  • Do not erase the original value after quarantine.

title: Backfill prompts: bound batches and make retries idempotent
summary: Use stable keys, durable checkpoints, and a rule for concurrent updates.
body:
A backfill prompt should state the ordering key, batch size, idempotent write rule, checkpoint contents, retry behavior, and rate limit. A checkpoint means a range was processed under a mapping version, not that its values are correct. The migration runner executes reviewed code; a model merely drafts a runbook. Preserve row versions where concurrent writes matter. A retry must not create a second target row or overwrite a newer source change with an older snapshot value.

Operational case

Harbor processes the 46,940 mappable rows in bounded key ranges. If a worker stops after committing a range, it resumes from the last durable checkpoint, and replaying that range yields the same target identity. The 60 quarantined rows remain in a separate owner queue. A source status update during the backfill is applied by the later change tail rather than being erased by a stale retry.

Batch key: tenant_id + order_id
Checkpoint: committed key + mapping version + watermark
Retry: same target identity, no duplicate insert
Concurrent change: compare version or replay tail

Performance and review cost

Processing N rows in batches of B is O(N) row work with about O(N/B) checkpoint writes, aside from index and network cost. Small batches shorten locks but increase overhead. Monitor latency and replication lag; a compact generated loop can still overload a live database.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call checkpoint completion value parity.
  • Do not let retries create new target IDs.
  • Do not overwrite a newer change with stale snapshot data.

title: Backfill prompts: account for writes during migration
summary: Define one write owner and a replay watermark for the live tail.
body:
A live backfill must account for changes after its snapshot through a write pause, controlled dual write, or ordered change-stream replay. The prompt should ask which system owns writes, how updates and deletes are represented, what watermark marks a complete tail, and how lag is observed. A zero-lag screenshot is not a durable completion claim if more events can arrive. The cutover plan needs an explicit stable gate and divergence monitoring after traffic changes.

Operational case

Harbor leaves the legacy table as write owner during snapshot H-47. New order updates enter an ordered tail that the target replays after backfill, including changes to quarantined IDs. The operator records the last applied watermark and measured lag at the planned cutover window. A generated paragraph cannot attest that the live stream is caught up; the running system supplies that evidence.

Write owner: legacy table
Snapshot: H-47 | tail: ordered positions
Update/delete: stable order key + source version
Cutover gate: measured lag and replay watermark

Performance and review cost

Applying T tail events is O(T) expected keyed work after O(N) snapshot processing. Stream ordering and deduplication may add cost. Controlled dual write can introduce partial-failure states, so any selected strategy needs a recovery path and observable lag receipt.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not ignore post-snapshot updates.
  • Do not give two systems write ownership without a conflict rule.
  • Do not claim the tail is complete without a watermark.

title: Backfill prompts: compare count and field-level parity
summary: Expose wrong values even when destination row counts match.
body:
Count parity is necessary but weak. A validation prompt should request the fixed source population, mapped and quarantined counts, destination unique-key count, duplicate-key check, field comparison, and mismatch ledger. Hashes help only when both sides use the same canonical encoding and field set. Keep row IDs for every mismatch. Reconcile all groups to the source total; a target with the right number of rows can still contain wrong statuses.

Operational case

Harbor has 47,000 source rows: 46,940 mapped and 60 quarantined. The target has 46,940 rows, so eligible count parity passes. A keyed status comparison finds three wrong values, leaving 46,937 matching. The model's report states both facts and withholds the cutover claim. An engineer checks whether mapping logic or retry ordering caused the three errors, then reruns the affected and full-population checks.

47,000 = 46,940 mapped + 60 quarantined
46,940 target = 46,937 matching + 3 mismatched
Count gate: pass | field-value gate: fail
Cutover: blocked

Performance and review cost

Sorting both N-row sets by key costs O(N log N); an indexed merge is O(N) after index preparation. Hash comparison is O(N) expected time and O(N) memory. The extra read pass reveals errors that a total cannot, and the three keyed IDs make the repair check specific.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not equate equal counts with equal values.
  • Do not compare hashes with different field encodings.
  • Do not omit quarantined rows from source reconciliation.

title: Backfill prompts: hold cutover until fallback is rehearsed
summary: Tie release to value checks, tail lag, owner approval, and a safe return path.
body:
A cutover packet needs mapping disposition, row and value parity, tail lag, read-path tests, capacity, rollback route, decision owner, and communications. The prompt drafts a checklist; it does not execute a switch. A fallback must account for writes accepted after any switch, since restoring an old backup alone may lose them. Keep private row content in the approved system and pass only counts, pseudonymous exception IDs, and synthetic examples into review text. Record a new receipt after the actual operation.

Operational case

Harbor still has 60 undispositioned source rows and three wrong target values. The decision is hold; the legacy table remains write owner. The operator rehearses a return route and a plan for post-switch writes in a representative environment. After owners resolve the 60 and three, a fresh parity and tail check can support a new approval. The assistant cannot label a plan as a completed cutover or paste tenant records into the memo.

Open: 47 unknown + 13 tenant missing + 3 value mismatches
Current write owner: legacy
Private rows: stay in controlled system
Fallback: preserve post-switch writes
Decision: hold until fresh approval and receipt

Performance and review cost

Checking G measured release gates is O(G) lookups, but rehearsal and fallback capacity dominate elapsed time. A summary built from E exceptions and B batch receipts costs O(E+B) ledger work. The slower operator gate protects data that is harder to recover than a draft paragraph.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not cut over from matching row counts alone.
  • Do not promise rollback without handling post-switch writes.
  • Do not expose full tenant rows to a planning prompt by default.

title: Project: review Harbor's order-status backfill
summary: Apply the database backfill evidence contract to a fictional packet.
body:
Review a fictional Harbor Orders migration from legacy status text to a typed status field. The model drafts mapping and validation plans. The migration runner and authorized operator control writes. Count parity alone does not establish value equivalence, tail completion, or safe cutover.

Review the packet

Snapshot H-47 contains 47,000 orders. The approved mapping handles 46,940; 60 are quarantined, comprising 47 unknown legacy statuses and 13 rows missing a tenant ID. The destination holds 46,940 rows after backfill, but three fail a field-level comparison. Thus 46,937 mapped rows currently match. Harbor holds cutover, assigns the 60 exceptions and three mismatches, and plans a fresh validation after repair. Writes continue in the legacy table; change-tail position and lag must also be verified before any switch.

Source snapshot 47,000 = mapped 46,940 + quarantined 60
Quarantine: 47 unknown status + 13 tenant ID missing
Destination 46,940 = matching 46,937 + mismatched 3
Current write owner: legacy table
Decision: hold cutover; resolve exceptions and tail

Performance and review cost

Scanning N source rows and writing eligible rows is O(N) application work, with database I/O and index maintenance often dominating. Field comparison adds another O(N) pass, and live-tail replay depends on concurrent write volume. Keep row-level exception IDs and a watermark so retries remain bounded and failed cutovers can be investigated without reconstructing the whole run.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call 46,940 destination rows 46,940 validated matches.
  • Do not map unknown statuses to a convenient default.
  • Do not cut over while value mismatches, exceptions, and tail evidence remain unresolved.

title: Search prompts: define query intent and evaluation slices
summary: Pin the user task, query population, and catalog snapshot before judging results.
body:
A search evaluation slice is a fixed set of queries grouped by the task the user meant to complete. Record normalized query text, language, device or role when relevant, intent class, catalog snapshot, filters, and expected eligible result type. A prompt may propose intent labels, but it must expose ambiguous queries and preserve the raw wording. A slice drawn only from successful searches cannot measure empty searches or uncommon terminology. The denominator belongs to the query set, not the number of results retrieved.

Operational case

Beacon Supply freezes 47 help and catalog queries at snapshot C-47. Five have no eligible result; they stay in the slice. A query for 'seal 47' may mean a part number or an installation guide, so reviewers keep both candidate intents until a session or owner clarifies the task. The model writes a proposed label and its evidence, not a made-up purchase intent. Role-specific filters are logged with the query because they change what could have been returned.

query_id: BS-Q47
raw_text: seal 47
intent_candidates: part lookup | installation help
catalog_snapshot: C-47
role_filter: contractor
intent_status: review

Performance and review cost

Grouping Q queries by a small intent taxonomy is O(Q) record work plus human review for ambiguous cases. Snapshotting the eligible catalog costs storage proportional to indexed records, but prevents later catalog changes from rewriting the test. Retain rare and zero-result queries even if their count makes a headline score less flattering.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not discard empty queries from the denominator.
  • Do not label ambiguity as certainty because one result looks plausible.
  • Do not compare slices built from different catalog snapshots.

title: Search prompts: judge relevance without treating unknown as wrong
summary: Build a candidate pool and a relevance rubric with an explicit unjudged state.
body:
A relevance rubric describes what counts as useful for a particular query and intent: exact answer, partial support, related but insufficient, or ineligible. Pool candidates from more than one retrieval or ranking variant so an incumbent system does not define the entire answer key. Every query-document pair needs a stable ID, snapshot, eligibility decision, grade, and judge status. Unjudged is a missing label. It is not the same as a human decision that a document fails the task.

Operational case

For Beacon's 'seal 47' query, a part page and an installation guide enter the candidate pool from different runs. The part page is useful only if the intent is product lookup; the guide is useful for installation help. A third result has not been reviewed. The prompt asks judges to cite the supported task, and the sheet keeps that third result unjudged until review. Seven disputed pairs have separate adjudication IDs rather than being flattened to a majority vote.

BS-Q47 / doc-P17: candidate grade, intent-dependent
BS-Q47 / doc-G42: candidate grade, intent-dependent
BS-Q47 / doc-U63: UNJUDGED
judgment_version: J-47
conflicts: adjudication queue

Performance and review cost

Pooling R runs over Q queries at K results requires O(RQK) candidate visits before deduplication. Labeling unique pairs costs human time and a ledger of O(U) records for U unique pairs. Pooling reduces dependence on one run but cannot prove every relevant document was found; record the pool construction rule.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not score an unjudged pair as a negative.
  • Do not let a single system supply all candidate documents.
  • Do not merge relevance and permission eligibility into one opaque grade.

title: Search prompts: diagnose candidate coverage and zero results
summary: Separate an empty eligible set from ranking failure and locate the cause.
body:
Candidate coverage asks whether retrieval produced a potentially useful, permitted item before ranking rearranged the list. An empty result can follow a missing document, stale index, analyzer mismatch, overstrict filter, or permission rule. A prompt should request a bounded diagnostic ledger: query ID, index snapshot, normalized tokens, filter chain, eligible count at each gate, and known answer availability. It must not recommend bypassing access control simply because a relevant private item exists.

Operational case

Beacon has five empty queries among 47. Two have catalog records not yet indexed, one uses an alternate part spelling, one is filtered by a category condition, and one would match only a document the contractor role cannot access. These are fictional diagnostic findings for the project packet, not five identical ranking defects. The permission case remains empty for that role; the proposed fix is a safe public answer or clearer no-result message, not exposure of the private record.

47 queries: 42 with candidates + 5 empty
empty causes: index lag 2; spelling 1; filter 1; permission 1
permission empty: do not relax access rule
owner: index | analyzer | filter | content/permission

Performance and review cost

Tracing Q queries through G gates costs O(QG) logged gate checks when counts are available. Replaying full retrieval can be more expensive because it touches the index and filter services. Gate counts narrow the investigation, while missing diagnostics should stay unknown rather than be assigned a convenient cause.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call every zero-result query a ranking bug.
  • Do not bypass a permission filter for better coverage.
  • Do not guess a cause without gate-level evidence.
